papers.title: Vaccination for girls and women across the life course: Evidence-based recommendations for clinical practice and policy.
papers.abstract: Vaccination across the life course is a cornerstone of preventive health care for girls and women. Although WHO recommends completion of essential vaccines by adolescence, global coverage remains suboptimal. Vaccine-preventable diseases-including HPV-related cancers, vaginal, vulvar, anal, oropharyngeal, influenza, pertussis, hepatitis B, herpes zoster, and pneumococcal disease-continue to impose a disproportionate burden on girls and women, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and migrant populations. Key life stages, such as childhood (early and middle), adolescence, preconception, pregnancy, postpartum, midlife, and beyond, offer critical opportunities for immunization. Obstetricians, gynecologists, midwives, and other women's healthcare providers are uniquely positioned to integrate vaccination into routine care in all settings and influence vaccine acceptance. Strengthening vaccine advocacy within women's health care is essential to reduce preventable morbidity and mortality and advance health equity for girls and women globally. This paper presents evidence-based recommendations for equitable vaccination across the life course of girls and women, synthesizing guidance from WHO, the Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization (SAGE), the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and national immunization technical advisory groups. Vaccines reviewed include HPV, tetanus-diphtheria-pertussis (Tdap), influenza, hepatitis B, measles-mumps-rubella (MMR), varicella, herpes zoster, pneumococcal, Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), and COVID-19. A life-course framework is proposed, emphasizing maternal immunization, cervical cancer prevention, and integration of regular and opportune vaccination into routine obstetric and gynecologic services. Practical implementation strategies and policy recommendations are outlined to support FIGO member societies.

papers.title: Multiple Sclerosis and Viruses: « Liaisons Dangereuses ».
papers.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a complex, multifactorial neurodegenerative disease with an aetiology that is still partially elusive. Several risk factors are associated with MS development including genetic predisposition and various environmental stressors; however, recently, viral infections have gained significant attention as a crucial environmental trigger. Despite the well-established link between Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and MS susceptibility, a single-pathogen model fails to clearly characterise the molecular cascades driving the disease, suggesting that the transition from infection to autoimmune response involves more than one viral agent. In this review we examine the speculation that the interactions among different neurotropic viruses could serve a collective causative role in MS, which is under-researched in the literature at present. We summarise contradictory evidence on the role of different viral agents, including the Herpesviridae family (Human Cytomegalovirus, EBV, Herpes Simplex Viruses HSV-1 and HSV-2, and Varicella Zoster Virus), Paramyxoviridae family (Measles Virus and Rubella Virus), Influenza virus, SARS-CoV-2, and Human Endogenous Retroviruses (HERVs). Through interplay within shared molecular pathways, immune modulation, and activation of latent infections, these viruses may collectively influence the inflammatory and demyelinating processes that characterise MS. This review evaluates the etiological role of viral interplay in MS through the cumulative and interactive effects of these pathogens. The available epidemiological, immunological, and experimental data converge on the concept that viral co-exposures act synergistically to shape MS susceptibility in genetically predisposed individuals. Characterising these viral interactions presents a new research direction for the identification of novel biomarkers and the development of preventative strategies through the targeted control of viral networks.

Despite the well-established link between Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and MS susceptibility, a single-pathogen model fails to clearly characterise the molecular cascades driving the disease, suggesting that the transition from infection to autoimmune response involves more than one viral agent. Characterising these viral interactions presents a new research direction for the identification of novel biomarkers and the development of preventative strategies through the targeted control of viral networks.

papers.abstract_zh: 多发性硬化症(MS)是一种复杂的、多因素的神经退行性疾病,其病因仍部分不明。与MS发病相关的风险因素包括遗传易感性和多种环境应激因素;然而,最近病毒感染引起了广泛关注,被认为是重要的环境诱因。尽管已知EB病毒(EBV)与MS易感性之间存在明确的关联,但单一病原体模型无法清晰描述驱动该疾病分子级联反应的机制,这表明从感染到自身免疫反应的转变可能涉及不止一种病毒。在本综述中,我们探讨了不同神经嗜性病毒之间的相互作用可能在MS中发挥协同致病作用的假设,这一领域目前在文献中研究较少。我们总结了不同病毒在MS发病中作用的矛盾证据,包括疱疹病毒科(人类巨细胞病毒、EB病毒、单纯疱疹病毒HSV-1和HSV-2,以及水痘-带状疱疹病毒)、副粘病毒科(麻疹病毒病毒和风疹病毒)、流感病毒、SARS-CoV-2以及人类内源性逆转录病毒(HERVs)。这些病毒可能通过在共享分子通路中的相互作用、免疫调节以及激活潜伏感染,共同影响MS中特征性的炎症和脱髓鞘过程。本综述评估了病毒相互作用在MS病因中的作用,通过这些病原体的累积和交互效应。现有的流行病学、免疫学和实验数据表明,病毒的共同暴露可能在遗传易感个体中协同影响MS的易感性。明确这些病毒相互作用为识别新型生物标志物和通过靶向控制病毒网络开发预防策略提供了新的研究方向。

papers.title: Oncolytic virotherapy for cancer: biological mechanisms, clinical advances, and future perspectives
papers.abstract: Abstract Oncolytic virotherapy has emerged as a promising cancer treatment that combines selective tumor destruction with potent stimulation of antitumor immunity. Unlike conventional therapies, oncolytic viruses (OVs) preferentially infect and replicate within malignant cells while sparing normal tissues, leading to direct tumor lysis and the release of tumor-associated antigens, pathogen-associated molecular patterns, and damage-associated molecular patterns that activate both innate and adaptive immune responses. Advances in molecular virology and genetic engineering have transformed naturally occurring viruses into programmable therapeutic platforms capable of delivering immunomodulatory payloads that enhance antitumor efficacy and remodel the tumor microenvironment. Multiple DNA- and RNA-based viral platforms, including herpes simplex virus, adenovirus, vaccinia virus, reovirus, measles virus, Newcastle disease virus, vesicular stomatitis virus, and coxsackievirus, are currently under clinical investigation, with regulatory approval of talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC) and G47Δ providing important proof of clinical feasibility. Increasing evidence indicates that OVs can convert immunologically "cold" tumors into "hot" tumors, thereby improving responsiveness to immune checkpoint inhibitors and other therapeutic modalities. Consequently, oncolytic virotherapy has become an attractive component of combination strategies involving immunotherapy, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted therapies, and cellular therapies. Nevertheless, several challenges continue to limit its broader clinical application, including antiviral immune clearance, inefficient systemic delivery, restricted intratumoral spread, tumor heterogeneity, manufacturing complexity, and the lack of robust predictive biomarkers. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the biological foundations of oncolytic virotherapy, viral engineering strategies, mechanisms of tumor selectivity, direct oncolysis, immunogenic cell death, and immune remodeling of the tumor microenvironment. It further summarizes the major oncolytic virus platforms, recent preclinical and clinical advances, emerging combination strategies, current translational challenges, and future directions expected to advance precision oncolytic virotherapy and expand its role in modern cancer treatment. Graphical Abstract Comprehensive overview of oncolytic virotherapy (OVT) from fundamental biology to clinical translation

papers.full_text: Abstract Oncolytic virotherapy has emerged as a promising cancer treatment that combines selective tumor destruction with potent stimulation of antitumor immunity. Consequently, oncolytic virotherapy has become an attractive component of combination strategies involving immunotherapy, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted therapies, and cellular therapies. Nevertheless, several challenges continue to limit its broader clinical application, including antiviral immune clearance, inefficient systemic delivery, restricted intratumoral spread, tumor heterogeneity, manufacturing complexity, and the lack of robust predictive biomarkers. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the biological foundations of oncolytic virotherapy, viral engineering strategies, mechanisms of tumor selectivity, direct oncolysis, immunogenic cell death, and immune remodeling of the tumor microenvironment. It further summarizes the major oncolytic virus platforms, recent preclinical and clinical advances, emerging combination strategies, current translational challenges, and future directions expected to advance precision oncolytic virotherapy and expand its role in modern cancer treatment. Graphical Abstract Comprehensive overview of oncolytic virotherapy (OVT) from fundamental biology to clinical translation Introduction Cancer remains one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide despite remarkable advances in diagnosis and treatment [1]. According to recent global estimates, nearly 20 million new cancer cases and approximately 10 million cancer-related deaths occur annually, and these numbers are expected to increase substantially over the coming decades owing to population aging and continued demographic growth [2]. Although improvements in screening, surgery, radiotherapy, systemic chemotherapy, targeted therapies, and immunotherapy have significantly improved patient outcomes in several malignancies, durable disease control remains elusive for many patients with advanced or metastatic cancer [3, 4]. Tumor heterogeneity, therapeutic resistance, immune evasion, and treatment-associated toxicities continue to limit the long-term effectiveness of current therapeutic strategies, highlighting the urgent need for more selective and durable anticancer approaches [5, 6]. Among recent advances in cancer therapy, immunotherapy has fundamentally changed the treatment landscape by harnessing the patient's immune system to recognize and eliminate malignant cells [7]. Immune checkpoint inhibitors, adoptive cell therapies, and cancer vaccines have produced remarkable and durable responses in selected patient populations. However, the clinical benefits of these approaches remain restricted to a subset of patients because many tumors possess an immunosuppressive microenvironment characterized by poor immune-cell infiltration, impaired antigen presentation, and multiple mechanisms of immune escape. These so-called "cold" tumors often respond poorly to existing immunotherapies, emphasizing the need for therapeutic strategies capable of simultaneously destroying tumor cells and stimulating effective antitumor immunity [8,9,10]. Oncolytic virotherapy has emerged as one of the most promising immunotherapeutic platforms to address these challenges [11]. Unlike conventional anticancer therapies that primarily target tumor cell proliferation or specific oncogenic pathways, oncolytic viruses (OVs) selectively infect, replicate within, and lyse malignant cells while largely sparing normal tissues. Viral replication within tumors not only induces direct cancer cell destruction but also initiates a cascade of immunological events that convert dying tumors into highly immunogenic sites. The release of tumor-associated antigens together with pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) promotes dendritic-cell activation, antigen presentation, and the subsequent induction of both innate and adaptive antitumor immune responses. Consequently, OVs function as dual-action therapeutics that combine direct oncolysis with immune-mediated tumor eradication [11, 12]. The concept of using viruses to treat cancer originated more than a century ago following observations that some patients experienced transient tumor regression after naturally acquired viral infections [13]. However, the clinical application of this concept remained limited until advances in molecular virology and genetic engineering enabled the development of viruses with enhanced tumor selectivity, improved safety, and greater therapeutic efficacy. These technological advances transformed naturally occurring viruses into programmable therapeutic platforms capable of delivering immunostimulatory molecules, cytokines, checkpoint inhibitors, tumor suppressors, and other therapeutic payloads directly to the tumor microenvironment [14,15,16]. Today, oncolytic virotherapy represents a rapidly evolving field at the intersection of virology, immunology, genetic engineering, and precision oncology [11]. A wide variety of DNA and RNA viruses have been developed as oncolytic platforms, including herpes simplex virus, adenovirus, vaccinia virus, reovirus, measles virus, Newcastle disease virus, vesicular stomatitis virus, and coxsackievirus. Each platform possesses distinct biological characteristics that influence tumor selectivity, genome engineering capacity, immune activation, and delivery strategies [17, 18, 19]. Among these, genetically modified herpes simplex virus has achieved the greatest clinical success, culminating in regulatory approval of talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC) for advanced melanoma and G47Δ for malignant glioma in Japan. These milestones have provided important clinical proof of concept that engineered viruses can be translated into effective cancer therapeutics [20, 21]. Increasing evidence now indicates that the therapeutic activity of OVs extends far beyond direct tumor lysis. Viral infection remodels the tumor microenvironment by promoting immune-cell recruitment, enhancing antigen presentation, stimulating inflammatory cytokine production, and reversing local immunosuppression [11, 22, 23]. Through these mechanisms, OVs can convert immunologically "cold" tumors into "hot" tumors that are more responsive to immune checkpoint blockade and other immunotherapies. This ability has positioned oncolytic virotherapy as an attractive partner for combination treatment strategies involving immune checkpoint inhibitors, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted therapies, cellular immunotherapies, and emerging precision medicine approaches [11, 16, 18]. Despite substantial progress, several important challenges continue to limit the widespread clinical implementation of oncolytic virotherapy. Host antiviral immunity can rapidly neutralize therapeutic viruses following systemic administration, reducing tumor delivery and persistence. In addition, the dense extracellular matrix, abnormal tumor vasculature, and highly heterogeneous tumor microenvironment can restrict viral dissemination within solid tumors [24, 25]. Manufacturing complexity, biomarker identification, optimal patient selection, and the design of effective combination regimens also remain major obstacles to broader clinical translation [26, 27]. Consequently, improving viral engineering, developing innovative delivery systems, identifying predictive biomarkers, and optimizing rational combination therapies have become major priorities in the next generation of OV research [27, 28]. Collectively, these advances have shifted the perception of oncolytic viruses from simple tumor-lytic agents to multifunctional immunotherapeutic platforms capable of integrating direct cytotoxicity with immune modulation. Rather than serving solely as stand-alone therapies, OVs are increasingly viewed as versatile components of multimodal cancer treatment designed to enhance the efficacy of existing therapeutic modalities while overcoming resistance mechanisms [11, 29]. In this review article, we provide a comprehensive overview of the biological principles underlying oncolytic virotherapy, including viral engineering strategies, mechanisms of tumor selectivity, direct oncolysis, immunogenic cell death, and immune remodeling of the tumor microenvironment. We further discuss the major oncolytic virus platforms, summarize current preclinical and clinical advances, evaluate combination strategies with established cancer therapies, examine the principal biological and translational challenges facing the field, and highlight emerging technologies that are expected to shape the next generation of precision oncolytic virotherapy. Principles and Mechanisms of Oncolytic Virotherapy Oncolytic virotherapy is based on the ability of selected viruses to preferentially infect, replicate within, and destroy cancer cells while sparing most normal tissues. Unlike conventional anticancer therapies that primarily induce direct cytotoxicity, oncolytic viruses (OVs) exert their therapeutic effects through two complementary mechanisms. First, they selectively replicate in malignant cells, leading to direct tumor destruction. Second, viral infection transforms the tumor into an inflammatory microenvironment that stimulates innate and adaptive immune responses against the cancer. Consequently, the therapeutic efficacy of modern oncolytic virotherapy depends not only on efficient viral replication but also on the generation of durable systemic antitumor immunity [28, 30,31,32,33,34]. Current evidence supports a unified mechanistic model in which therapeutic activity proceeds through sequential but interconnected events. Initially, OVs selectively target susceptible tumor cells and establish productive viral replication. This replication results in direct tumor cell lysis and the release of newly generated viral particles, enabling infection to spread throughout the tumor. Simultaneously, dying cancer cells release tumor-associated antigens (TAAs), pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), cytokines, and chemokines. Together, these molecules activate innate immune cells, promote antigen presentation, and stimulate tumor-specific T-cell responses that extend antitumor activity beyond the sites of viral infection. Thus, contemporary oncolytic virotherapy is increasingly recognized as both a targeted cytotoxic therapy and an in situ cancer vaccination strategy [30, 33, 35]. Selective Tumor Targeting (Viral Tropism) Selective tumor targeting represents the fundamental principle underlying oncolytic virotherapy. Successful treatment requires viruses to infect and replicate preferentially within malignant cells while minimizing infection of healthy tissues. This selectivity results from a combination of natural viral tropism, cancer-associated cellular abnormalities, characteristics of the tumor microenvironment, and genetic engineering approaches that further enhance tumor specificity [30, 34, 36, 37]. Natural viral tropism Natural viral tropism refers to the inherent preference of a virus for specific cell types based on the interaction between viral surface proteins and host-cell receptors. Many cancers overexpress receptors that facilitate viral attachment and entry, making malignant cells more susceptible to infection than normal tissues [11, 38]. Several clinically important OVs exploit these receptor differences. Adenovirus serotype 5 primarily enters cells through the coxsackievirus and adenovirus receptor (CAR), whereas alternative adenoviral serotypes and chimeric vectors, including Ad3 and Ad5/35, preferentially utilize CD46 or desmoglein-2 (DSG2), thereby broadening their infectivity across different tumor types [16, 37, 39]. Measles virus targets CD46 and signaling lymphocytic activation molecule (SLAM), both of which are frequently upregulated in malignant tissues. Herpes simplex virus (HSV) enters cells through herpesvirus entry mediator (HVEM) and nectin-1 or nectin-2 receptors, whereas poliovirus selectively infects cells expressing CD155, a receptor that is highly expressed in numerous solid tumors and hematological malignancies [11, 18, 40]. Similarly, coxsackievirus A11 preferentially infects thoracic malignancies through intercellular adhesion molecule−1 (ICAM-1), illustrating how receptor expression can determine tumor susceptibility to specific viral platforms [41]. Although receptor abundance strongly influences viral entry, receptor expression alone does not determine therapeutic success. Productive infection also depends on the ability of tumor cells to support efficient viral replication after viral entry [11, 42]. Intracellular permissiveness Following entry into the cell, OVs rely on the intracellular environment to complete their replication cycle (Fig. 1). Cancer cells frequently harbor genetic and signaling abnormalities that unintentionally create conditions favorable for viral replication while weakening antiviral defense mechanisms [11, 43]. Activation of oncogenic pathways, including Ras, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), Wnt/β-catenin, phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/AKT, and defects in the p53, retinoblastoma (RB)/E2F, ATM, and apoptotic signaling pathways, supports viral replication by increasing cellular metabolic activity, promoting protein synthesis, and reducing antiviral responses [11, 36, 40]. Consequently, malignant cells become substantially more permissive to viral infection than normal cells. Reovirus provides one of the best-characterized examples of this mechanism. In tumors with activated Ras signaling, antiviral protein kinase R (PKR) activity is suppressed, allowing efficient viral protein translation and replication. At the same time, Ras activation reduces type I interferon-mediated antiviral responses, enabling selective viral propagation within malignant cells while normal tissues retain effective antiviral protection [17, 18]. Similarly, many tumors exhibit defects in innate immune sensing pathways, particularly the cyclic GMP–AMP synthase–stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS–STING) pathway and type I interferon signaling. These defects impair the ability of cancer cells to detect and eliminate viral infection, thereby providing a permissive environment for OV replication. In contrast, healthy tissues generally preserve intact antiviral signaling, limiting viral replication and contributing to the favorable safety profile of many clinically developed OVs [30, 44, 45]. Influence of the tumor microenvironment The tumor microenvironment (TME) further contributes to selective viral targeting. Unlike normal tissues, solid tumors are characterized by hypoxia, abnormal vascular architecture, nutrient deprivation, oxidative stress, and chronic inflammation. These conditions alter cellular metabolism and gene expression, creating an environment that often favors viral replication [33, 46]. Hypoxia is particularly important because activation of hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1) signaling promotes transcriptional programs that enhance viral gene expression and replication in several OV platforms. In addition, impaired immune surveillance within many tumors reduces early viral clearance, allowing viruses to spread more efficiently through malignant tissue than through healthy organs [36, 45]. Consequently, both intrinsic cellular defects and unique microenvironmental conditions cooperate to enhance tumor-selective viral replication. Engineering strategies to improve tumor selectivity Although many OVs possess inherent tumor selectivity, modern virotherapy increasingly relies on genetic engineering to improve specificity, maximize therapeutic efficacy, and reduce off-target toxicity (Table 1). These modifications have transformed naturally occurring viruses into highly programmable therapeutic platforms [16, 17]. Receptor retargeting modifies viral attachment proteins to redirect viral entry toward receptors that are preferentially expressed on tumor cells. Examples include adenoviral vectors engineered to utilize CD46 instead of CAR and HSV-1 vectors retargeted toward epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) or nectin-1, thereby improving infection of tumors with limited susceptibility to their native viruses [18, 40]. Transcriptional targeting restricts viral gene expression to malignant cells by placing essential viral genes under the control of tumor-selective promoters, such as those derived from human telomerase reverse transcriptase (hTERT) or survivin. Because these promoters exhibit minimal activity in most normal tissues, viral replication remains largely confined to cancer cells, thereby enhancing safety [47, 48]. analysis.summary_en: This review explores the potential of oncolytic virotherapy, particularly using measles virus, as a promising cancer treatment. It highlights the biological mechanisms of oncolytic viruses, their ability to stimulate antitumor immunity, and their role in converting immunologically cold tumors into hot ones. The review also discusses the clinical advances, including the approval of T-VEC and G47Δ, and the challenges such as immune clearance and manufacturing complexity. It emphasizes the importance of measles virus in combination strategies with immunotherapy, chemotherapy, and other modalities. The review concludes with future directions aimed at improving precision and expanding the use of oncolytic virotherapy in cancer treatment.

papers.abstract_zh: 摘要 肿瘤溶细胞病毒治疗(OVT)作为一种结合选择性肿瘤破坏与强效抗肿瘤免疫刺激的癌症治疗方式,展现出巨大的前景。与传统疗法不同,溶细胞病毒(OVs)能够选择性地感染并复制于恶性细胞中,同时避免对正常组织的损害,从而直接导致肿瘤裂解,并释放肿瘤相关抗原、病原体相关分子模式以及损伤相关分子模式,激活先天性和适应性免疫应答。分子病毒学和基因工程领域的进展,已将天然病毒转化为可编程的治疗平台,能够递送免疫调节性载荷,增强抗肿瘤效果并重塑肿瘤微环境。目前,多种基于DNA和RNA的病毒平台,包括单纯疱疹病毒、腺病毒、牛痘病毒、轮状病毒、麻疹病毒、新城疫病毒、水疱性口炎病毒以及柯萨奇病毒,均在临床研究中,其中talimogene laherparepvec(T-VEC)和G47Δ的监管批准为临床可行性提供了重要证据。越来越多的证据表明,OVs能够将免疫学上“冷”的肿瘤转化为“热”肿瘤,从而提高其对免疫检查点抑制剂及其他治疗方式的响应性。因此,溶细胞病毒治疗已成为结合免疫治疗、化疗、放疗、靶向治疗和细胞治疗等综合策略中的一个有吸引力的组成部分。然而,一些挑战仍然限制了其更广泛的应用,包括抗病毒药物免疫清除、系统性递送效率低下、肿瘤内扩散受限、肿瘤异质性、制造复杂性以及缺乏可靠的预测性生物标志物。本综述全面概述了溶细胞病毒治疗的生物基础,包括病毒工程策略、肿瘤选择性机制、直接溶细胞作用、免疫源性细胞死亡以及肿瘤微环境的免疫重塑。此外,还总结了主要的溶细胞病毒平台、近期的临床前和临床进展、新兴的联合治疗策略、当前的转化挑战以及未来方向,旨在推动精准溶细胞病毒治疗的发展,并拓展其在现代癌症治疗中的作用。图形摘要 溶细胞病毒治疗(OVT)从基础生物学到临床转化的全面概述

papers.title: Vaccine Response Assessment in Children Using Dried Blood Spots: The DRIVE Study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Dried blood spots (DBS) are a minimally invasive alternative to serum for serological surveillance, but pediatric data remain limited, particularly in high-resource settings and in immunocompromised children. We evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of DBS for assessing vaccine-induced immunity in a pediatric cohort from Madrid, Spain. METHODS: This prospective observational study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of DBS compared with serum samples in 134 children and adolescents (98 nonimmunocompromised, 36 immunocompromised) at La Paz University Hospital (Madrid, Spain). IgG antibodies against 6 vaccine-preventable diseases-diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, measles, mumps, and rubella-were quantified using the VirClia® IgG chemiluminescence assay. ROC curves were constructed to establish optimal DBS cutoff values for each pathogen. RESULTS: Using serum cutoffs, DBS showed sensitivities >95% and specificities >85% for all pathogens, except for pertussis, which had a sensitivity of 66.7%, and for rubella and mumps, which had specificities of 62.5% and 44.0%, respectively. Applying optimized DBS cutoffs improved specificity for rubella (81.2%) and mumps (88.0%). In immunocompromised children, sensitivity remained >80% for most pathogens but decreased for mumps (76.0%). Age and time since vaccination did not significantly affect DBS performance. CONCLUSIONS: Dried blood spot provide a reliable and practical approach for assessing vaccine-induced immunity in children and adolescents. Their ease of collection and transport make them especially valuable in settings with limited laboratory capacity. Population-specific cutoffs are essential, particularly for immunocompromised groups, to ensure diagnostic accuracy and support global immunization monitoring.

papers.title_zh: 使用干血斑评估儿童疫苗反应:DRIVE研究。
papers.source_body_en: BACKGROUND: Dried blood spots (DBS) are a minimally invasive alternative to serum for serological surveillance, but pediatric data remain limited, particularly in high-resource settings and in immunocompromised children. We evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of DBS for assessing vaccine-induced immunity in a pediatric cohort from Madrid, Spain. METHODS: This prospective observational study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of DBS compared with serum samples in 134 children and adolescents (98 nonimmunocompromised, 36 immunocompromised) at La Paz University Hospital (Madrid, Spain). IgG antibodies against 6 vaccine-preventable diseases-diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, measles, mumps, and rubella-were quantified using the VirClia® IgG chemiluminescence assay. ROC curves were constructed to establish optimal DBS cutoff values for each pathogen. RESULTS: Using serum cutoffs, DBS showed sensitivities >95% and specificities >85% for all pathogens, except for pertussis, which had a sensitivity of 66.7%, and for rubella and mumps, which had specificities of 62.5% and 44.0%, respectively. Applying optimized DBS cutoffs improved specificity for rubella (81.2%) and mumps (88.0%). In immunocompromised children, sensitivity remained >80% for most pathogens but decreased for mumps (76.0%). Age and time since vaccination did not significantly affect DBS performance. CONCLUSIONS: Dried blood spot provide a reliable and practical approach for assessing vaccine-induced immunity in children and adolescents. Their ease of collection and transport make them especially valuable in settings with limited laboratory capacity. Population-specific cutoffs are essential, particularly for immunocompromised groups, to ensure diagnostic accuracy and support global immunization monitoring.
papers.abstract_zh: 背景:干血斑(DBS)是血清的一种微创替代方法,用于血清学监测检测,但关于儿童的数据仍然有限,尤其是在高资源环境和免疫功能低下儿童中。我们评估了DBS在评估西班牙马德里La Paz大学医院中一名儿童队列研究所诱导的免疫力方面的诊断准确性。方法:这项前瞻性观察性研究在西班牙马德里La Paz大学医院的134名儿童和青少年(98名非免疫功能低下,36名免疫功能低下)中评估了DBS与血清样本相比的诊断准确性。使用VirClia® IgG化学发光检测法对6种疫苗可预防疾病的IgG抗体进行了定量分析,构建ROC曲线以确定每种病原体的最佳DBS截断值。结果:使用血清截断值,DBS对所有病原体的敏感性均大于95%,特异性均大于85%,除了百日咳(敏感性为66.7%)以及麻疹(特异性为44.0%)和腮腺炎(特异性为62.5%)。应用优化的DBS截断值提高了麻疹(81.2%)和腮腺炎(88.0%)的特异性。在免疫功能低下儿童中,大多数病原体的敏感性仍保持在80%以上,但麻疹的敏感性有所下降(76.0%)。年龄和接种疫苗接种后的时间对DBS性能没有显著影响。结论:干血斑为评估儿童和青少年疫苗诱导的免疫力提供了一种可靠且实用的方法。其采集和运输的简便性使其在实验室资源有限的环境中特别有价值。针对特定人群的截断值是确保诊断准确性和支持全球疫苗接种监测的关键。

papers.title: Emerging Trends of Infectious Diseases in Canada
papers.abstract: Emerging trends in infectious diseases in Canada reveal a dynamic landscape influenced by climate change, global travel, close interactions with livestock or wild animals, and increased antimicrobial resistance. Rising global temperatures and altered ecosystems have expanded the geographic range for key vector-borne diseases such as Lyme disease, tick-borne illnesses like anaplasmosis and babesiosis, and West Nile virus. Furthermore, urbanization and travel have complicated the overlapping interactions between humans, intermediate hosts (e.g., livestock and rodents), and insect/arthropod vectors. The resurgence of vaccine-preventable diseases post-pandemic, including measles and pertussis, underscores the critical role of immunization programs to manage downstream impacts of vaccine hesitancy. The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the need for robust public health infrastructure and preparedness to manage novel pathogens. Genomic surveillance and advanced diagnostics are enhancing the ability to detect and respond to outbreaks more swiftly. Additionally, the ongoing opioid crisis and disruptions to comprehensive healthcare have exacerbated the spread of bloodborne infections like HIV, hepatitis C, and tuberculosis among vulnerable populations. Moreover, Canada's multicultural population requires tailored public health strategies to address its diverse healthcare needs and disparities. Ongoing research, active surveillance, and interdisciplinary collaboration for clinical guidelines are essential to mitigate the impact of these emerging infectious diseases.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在探讨影响加拿大传染病爆发的因素,特别是关注疫情后麻疹及其他疫苗可预防传染病的再次出现。研究强调了理解气候变化、全球旅行和抗菌药物耐药性如何影响传染病动态景观的重要性。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究分析了加拿大传染病的新兴趋势,包括麻疹和百日咳的再次流行,并考察了气候变化、全球旅行和抗菌药物耐受性等因素对这些趋势的影响。此外,还考虑了疫苗接种计划在应对疫苗犹豫现象带来的下游效应中的作用。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究采用对现有文献和加拿大传染病趋势数据的回顾,重点关注疫情后麻疹和百日咳的再次流行。它分析了气候变化、全球旅行和抗菌药物耐药性对这些趋势的影响,并评估了免疫接种计划在减轻其影响中的作用。
elements_zh.main_results: 加拿大传染病的新兴趋势显示出一个动态的图景,受到气候变化、全球旅行、与家畜或野生动物的密切接触以及抗菌药物耐受性增加的影响。在疫情后,麻疹可预防的疾病如疫苗和百日咳的再次出现,突显了疫苗接种计划在应对疫苗犹豫所带来的下游影响中的关键作用。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 该研究将麻疹和百日咳的再次流行解释为疫苗犹豫不决以及免疫接种计划削弱的直接结果,强调需要强大的公共卫生基础设施来有效应对这些挑战。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果强调了维持和加强免疫接种计划以预防麻疹及其他疫苗可预防疾病的必要性,特别是在后疫情时代公共卫生准备的背景下。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究基于摘要证据,未提供详细的统计分析或具体的数值结果。然而,它提供了一个关于影响麻疹和百日咳病再度爆发的因素的一般概述,其结论具有中等程度的可信度。

papers.title: Associations between parental generative artificial intelligence health-advice use and child vaccination uptake in Japan: an exploratory cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parents increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (AI) for health information, but evidence on parental AI use and childhood vaccination is limited. We examined exploratory associations between regular parental AI health-advice use and childhood vaccination in Japan. METHODS: This cross-sectional study analyzed 2025 nationwide survey data from children aged 1 to 17 years and parents, with a linked 2023-2025 sub-analysis. The exposure was regular parental use of generative AI for health advice at least a few times per month. Outcomes were age-appropriate measles-rubella (MR) vaccination and any mumps, influenza, or coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) vaccination. Modified Poisson regression estimated adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) and 95% confidence interval (95% CI) with parent-level clustering and covariates. RESULTS: Among 8282 children and 5170 parents, 1278 (15.4%) had regular AI health-advice users as parents. AI use was not associated with age-appropriate MR vaccination (aPR 1.02; 95% CI 0.97-1.09), but was associated with three vaccines. The adjusted rates were 76.6 versus 72.7% (aPR 1.05, 95% CI 1.01-1.10) for mumps, 56.7% versus 49.0% (aPR 1.16, 95% CI 1.08-1.24) for influenza, 40.6% versus 30.9% (aPR 1.31, 95% CI 1.19-1.45) for COVID-19. The COVID-19 association was strongest among parents younger than 30 years (aPR 2.58; 95% CI 1.90-3.50; P for interaction < 0.001). In the linked sub-analysis, these associations persisted after adjustment for an available 2023 household-level prior vaccination marker and attitudes. CONCLUSIONS: Regular parental use of generative AI for health advice was associated with mumps, influenza, and COVID-19 vaccination, but not with age-appropriate MR vaccination. These exploratory, cross-sectional findings are observational associations. They may reflect digital health engagement, health information seeking, socioeconomic differences, or favorable attitudes, rather than vaccine-specific AI advice.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the association between parental use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) for health advice and child vaccination uptake in Japan. The cross-sectional analysis of 2025 nationwide survey data found that regular AI use was not linked to age-appropriate measles-rubella (MR) vaccination but was associated with increased uptake of mumps, influenza, and coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) vaccines. The strongest association was observed among parents younger than 30 years for COVID-19 vaccination. The study highlights potential links between digital health engagement and vaccination behavior, though it acknowledges the observational nature of the findings and possible confounding factors such as socioeconomic status and attitudes. These results may inform public health strategies aimed at leveraging digital tools to enhance vaccination rates, but further research is needed to establish causality and explore mechanisms.

papers.title: Application and prospects of veterinary diagnostic techniques in laboratory monkeys

source_records.title: Application and prospects of veterinary diagnostic techniques in laboratory monkeys
Application and prospects of veterinary diagnostic techniques in laboratory monkeys

papers.priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
papers.full_text: As the non-human primate models with the closest genetic relationship to humans, laboratory monkeys are indispensable in life sciences research, drug development, and biological product evaluation. However, infectious diseases either endemic in laboratory monkey colonies or acquired during breeding and husbandry—for example, B virus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis-threaten animal welfare and colony security, while also elevating zoonotic transmission risks and compromising the reliability of research data. The diversity, complexity, and clinically insidious nature of diseases in laboratory monkeys impose stringent demands on veterinary diagnostic capabilities. This review summarizes the current status and recent advances in mainstream veterinary diagnostic techniques applied to laboratory monkey disease surveillance. We analyze the specific applications, strengths, and limitations of molecular, immunological, imaging, and conventional microbiological methods for detecting major viral, bacterial, and parasitic pathogens of laboratory monkeys, covering quantitative PCR (qPCR), CRISPR-based assays, ELISA, IFA/IHC, and other established platforms. By comparing these techniques across sensitivity, specificity, cost-effectiveness, and operational feasibility, we delineate their suitability for distinct use cases: high-precision laboratory testing, large-scale colony screening, and point-of-care clinical diagnosis. Current veterinary diagnostic assays for laboratory monkeys achieve robust analytical performance. In several studies, qPCR delivers 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity for B virus detection, digital PCR (dPCR) attains a limit of detection as low as 45 copies/ml for monkeypox virus; and CRISPR/Cas-based assays have demonstrated 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity in clinical validation cohorts. Building on these advances, we further identify practical bottlenecks in diagnostic deployment and propose targeted countermeasures. Finally, we explore emerging trends and application prospects for point-of-care testing, multiplex pathogen detection, and artificial intelligence-assisted diagnosis, which collectively support the development of accurate, efficient, and intelligent disease diagnostics for laboratory monkeys. This work aims to provide a theoretical and practical reference for clinical practice and scientific research focused on laboratory monkey disease prevention and control. 7ConclusionVeterinary diagnostic techniques are essential for safeguarding the welfare of laboratory monkeys, maintaining biosafety, and ensuring the reliability of biomedical research data. Several key takeaways emerge from this review with direct practical implications.First, no single diagnostic technique is universally applicable. The choice of diagnostic method should be guided by the specific pathogen (e.g., bacterial, viral, or parasitic), sample type (e.g., blood, BALF, or tissue), and clinical scenario (e.g., routine screening, outbreak investigation, or confirmatory diagnosis). Second, combined diagnostic strategies that integrate molecular, immunological, imaging, and traditional microbiological approaches are more reliable than any single technology, as they provide complementary evidence across multiple diagnostic dimensions. Third, context-specific factors, including cost, equipment availability, operator expertise, and biosafety requirements, must be carefully weighed when selecting diagnostic approaches for different facility types.To properly evaluate and deploy emerging technologies in laboratory primates, three research priorities should be addressed. First, prospective validation studies with standardized protocols and well-defined reference standards are urgently needed to establish the true performance of new diagnostic platforms under real-world conditions. Second, multi-center collaboration across different NHP facilities is essential to generate robust and generalizable evidence that accounts for population diversity and institutional variability. Third, cost-effectiveness analyses should be conducted to inform practical deployment decisions, particularly for resource-limited settings where advanced technologies may be prohibitively expensive.In conclusion, the future of laboratory monkey diagnostics lies not in replacing established methods with emerging technologies, but in their strategic integration. Guided by clinical context and supported by rigorous validation, this integrated approach will enable accurate, efficient, and sustainable disease management that benefits both animal health and biomedical research. 1Hazards of infectious diseases in laboratory monkeysLaboratory monkeys, primarily including macaques, cynomolgus monkeys, and rhesus monkeys, are non-human primates (NHPs) that share a high degree of anatomical, physiological, genetic, and immunological similarity with humans. As a result, they have become indispensable key experimental animal resources in fundamental medical research, new drug and vaccine development, and disease model construction. However, the widespread use of laboratory monkeys is also accompanied by serious challenges in disease prevention and control. Laboratory monkey populations carry or are susceptible to a wide variety of pathogens, including highly pathogenic zoonotic agents (1, 2).B virus is widely prevalent in monkey populations, typically presenting a benign course, yet it poses a significant threat to human health, potentially causing encephalomyelitis with a case fatality rate as high as 40% (3, 4); Mycobacterium tuberculosis (TB) is also a common pathogen in laboratory monkeys, particularly in Old World monkeys. Tuberculosis not only causes morbidity and mortality in monkey colonies, leading to substantial economic losses, but also represents a serious zoonotic disease that threatens public health security (5, 6). In recent years, with the frequent occurrence of global public health events, emerging or re-emerging zoonotic viruses such as monkeypox virus have garnered significant attention. Their transmission and surveillance in monkey populations are of critical importance (7, 8). In addition, infections with pathogens such as Simian Immunodeficiency Virus (SIV), simian measles virus, Toxoplasma gondii, and Chlamydia spp. are also common in laboratory monkey populations. These infections may manifest as overt diseases or remain in latent or subclinical states (9–12). Gastrointestinal parasites have also been documented in macaque populations, with potential zoonotic implications (13).The presence of infectious diseases in laboratory monkeys directly compromises their animal welfare and health, affecting the stability and breeding of the population. Latent infections with pathogens may serve as uncontrolled confounding variables in experimental studies, impairing the accuracy, reproducibility, and reliability of research outcomes. They may even lead to erroneous judgments regarding the safety and efficacy of drugs or therapies. Therefore, the establishment and application of accurate, rapid, and efficient veterinary diagnostic techniques play a critical role in the early detection, precise identification, and effective surveillance of infectious diseases in laboratory monkeys.Beyond single-pathogen threats, the epidemiological reality in laboratory monkey colonies is further complicated by frequent co-infections. Studies have shown that co-infection with TB and Simian Retrovirus (SRV) is prevalent in macaque colonies-with SRV seroprevalence reaching 19~50% in some breeding colonies and TB infection rates as high as 30~45% in endemic facilities. Such co-infections can profoundly impact disease progression, immune responses, and experimental outcomes (2, 9, 14). Concurrent infections with B virus and SIV have also been reported, with B virus seroprevalence reaching 80~90% in adult macaques. SIV infection rates varying from 5 to 40% depending on geographic origin and housing conditions (3, 15, 16). Furthermore, a single macaque can be asymptomatically infected with multiple pathogens simultaneously. For example, co-infection rates of SIV with measles virus or Toxoplasma gondii have been documented at 10~30% in certain colonies (9–12, 17). Such co-infections create a complex network of latent infections that acts as an uncontrolled variable in experimental studies, impairing accuracy and reproducibility, and potentially leading to erroneous judgments regarding the safety and efficacy of drugs or therapies. The high prevalence of co - infections underscores the urgent need for diagnostic techniques capable of high - throughput, multiplex detection (18, 19).Previous reviews have addressed specific aspects of NHP diagnostics: Ohta focused on pathology (2), Yang et al. on viral detection (1), and Wolf et al. on TB testing (20). However, no previous review has integrated all four major diagnostic modalities within a single framework tailored specifically to laboratory monkeys. This Mini Review fills this gap by providing a comprehensive comparative overview across molecular, immunological, imaging, and traditional microbiological methods, clarifying scenario-specific suitability, identifying practical bottlenecks, and discussing emerging technologies. This work serves as a practical reference for veterinarians and researchers working with NHP models.The diagnosis of infectious diseases in laboratory monkeys carries significant biosafety and occupational health implications that must be carefully addressed. Specimen collection (e.g., blood, saliva, BALF, tissues) should be performed using appropriate restraint and sedation to minimize stress and injury risk. Specimen handling and transport must follow strict biosafety protocols to prevent aerosol generation, spills, and contamination. Containment measures-including biosafety cabinets, sealed centrifuges, and appropriate facility BSL levels-are essential when processing potentially infectious samples. Personal protective measures (e.g., gloves, gowns, face shields, N95 respirators) should be mandatory for all personnel handling monkey-derived specimens or performing necropsies. Decontamination of surfaces, equipment, and waste is critical to prevent environmental contamination. Occupational exposure management-including post-exposure prophylaxis for B virus, TB screening, and incident reporting systems-should be in place for all facilities housing laboratory monkeys (3). The integration of veterinary diagnostics with occupational-health monitoring ensures that diagnostic results from animals inform human health surveillance, creating a bidirectional safety net.These biosafety and occupational health considerations firmly embed laboratory-monkey diagnostics within the One Health framework. Robust diagnostic practices protect not only animal welfare by enabling early detection and treatment, but also occupational health by safeguarding facility personnel from zoonotic infections. They contribute to zoonotic disease prevention by identifying infected animals before transmission occurs, and to biosafety and biosecurity by containing pathogens at their source. Furthermore, accurate diagnostics enhance public-health surveillance for emerging zoonotic threats and ensure the reliability of biomedical research by maintaining specific-pathogen-free colonies and preventing undetected infections from confounding experimental data. Thus, veterinary diagnostics for laboratory monkeys represent a critical interface between animal and human health, embodying the core principles of One Health (21).To clearly demonstrate the novelty of this Mini Review, a structured comparison with previous reviews is warranted. Ohta (2) provided a comprehensive summary of pathologic characteristics of infectious diseases in macaques, with a focus on histopathological findings rather than diagnostic methodologies. Yang et al. (1) updated practices for viral detection in breeding macaques, primarily emphasizing molecular assays for specific viruses without coverage of other pathogen categories or non-molecular techniques. Wolf et al. (20) reviewed noninvasive testing strategies for tuberculosis detection in primates, but did not extend to other bacterial, viral, or parasitic pathogens. In contrast, this Mini Review integrates all four major diagnostic modalities-molecular, immunological, imaging, and traditional microbiological methods-across viral, bacterial, and parasitic diseases, and provides a comparative scenario-based framework and a practical diagnostic algorithm. This integrated approach, tailored specifically to the unique constraints of laboratory monkey diagnostics, distinguishes the present work from previous reviews.Consistent with the Mini Review format, this article does not include a formal systematic review methodology. 2Current status of diagnostic techniques2.1Limitations of traditional diagnostic techniquesPathogen isolation and culture have long been regarded as the definitive reference for the diagnosis of bacterial and viral diseases. They enable the recovery of live pathogens and provide a foundation for subsequent antimicrobial susceptibility testing and vaccine development. In the diagnosis of monkey tuberculosis, the isolation and culture of TB from suspicious specimens serve as the definitive basis for confirmation (22). However, traditional culture methods are time-consuming, labor-intensive, and require high-level biosafety facilities. Some pathogens are difficult to culture in vitro, which limits their application in rapid and large-scale screening. Quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR), owing to its high sensitivity, high specificity, and quantitative capability, has become the mainstream technology for the detection of viral and bacterial pathogens in laboratory monkeys. full_text_sections.abstract: As the non-human primate models with the closest genetic relationship to humans, laboratory monkeys are indispensable in life sciences research, drug development, and biological product evaluation. However, infectious diseases either endemic in laboratory monkey colonies or acquired during breeding and husbandry—for example, B virus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis-threaten animal welfare and colony security, while also elevating zoonotic transmission risks and compromising the reliability of research data. The diversity, complexity, and clinically insidious nature of diseases in laboratory monkeys impose stringent demands on veterinary diagnostic capabilities. This review summarizes the current status and recent advances in mainstream veterinary diagnostic techniques applied to laboratory monkey disease surveillance. We analyze the specific applications, strengths, and limitations of molecular, immunological, imaging, and conventional microbiological methods for detecting major viral, bacterial, and parasitic pathogens of laboratory monkeys, covering quantitative PCR (qPCR), CRISPR-based assays, ELISA, IFA/IHC, and other established platforms. By comparing these techniques across sensitivity, specificity, cost-effectiveness, and operational feasibility, we delineate their suitability for distinct use cases: high-precision laboratory testing, large-scale colony screening, and point-of-care clinical diagnosis. Current veterinary diagnostic assays for laboratory monkeys achieve robust analytical performance. In several studies, qPCR delivers 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity for B virus detection, digital PCR (dPCR) attains a limit of detection as low as 45 copies/ml for monkeypox virus; and CRISPR/Cas-based assays have demonstrated 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity in clinical validation cohorts. Building on these advances, we further identify practical bottlenecks in diagnostic deployment and propose targeted countermeasures. Finally, we explore emerging trends and application prospects for point-of-care testing, multiplex pathogen detection, and artificial intelligence-assisted diagnosis, which collectively support the development of accurate, efficient, and intelligent disease diagnostics for laboratory monkeys. This work aims to provide a theoretical and practical reference for clinical practice and scientific research focused on laboratory monkey disease prevention and control.
full_text_sections.conclusion: 7ConclusionVeterinary diagnostic techniques are essential for safeguarding the welfare of laboratory monkeys, maintaining biosafety, and ensuring the reliability of biomedical research data. Several key takeaways emerge from this review with direct practical implications.First, no single diagnostic technique is universally applicable. The choice of diagnostic method should be guided by the specific pathogen (e.g., bacterial, viral, or parasitic), sample type (e.g., blood, BALF, or tissue), and clinical scenario (e.g., routine screening, outbreak investigation, or confirmatory diagnosis). Second, combined diagnostic strategies that integrate molecular, immunological, imaging, and traditional microbiological approaches are more reliable than any single technology, as they provide complementary evidence across multiple diagnostic dimensions. Third, context-specific factors, including cost, equipment availability, operator expertise, and biosafety requirements, must be carefully weighed when selecting diagnostic approaches for different facility types.To properly evaluate and deploy emerging technologies in laboratory primates, three research priorities should be addressed. First, prospective validation studies with standardized protocols and well-defined reference standards are urgently needed to establish the true performance of new diagnostic platforms under real-world conditions. Second, multi-center collaboration across different NHP facilities is essential to generate robust and generalizable evidence that accounts for population diversity and institutional variability. Third, cost-effectiveness analyses should be conducted to inform practical deployment decisions, particularly for resource-limited settings where advanced technologies may be prohibitively expensive.In conclusion, the future of laboratory monkey diagnostics lies not in replacing established methods with emerging technologies, but in their strategic integration. Guided by clinical context and supported by rigorous validation, this integrated approach will enable accurate, efficient, and sustainable disease management that benefits both animal health and biomedical research.
full_text_sections.other: 1Hazards of infectious diseases in laboratory monkeysLaboratory monkeys, primarily including macaques, cynomolgus monkeys, and rhesus monkeys, are non-human primates (NHPs) that share a high degree of anatomical, physiological, genetic, and immunological similarity with humans. As a result, they have become indispensable key experimental animal resources in fundamental medical research, new drug and vaccine development, and disease model construction. However, the widespread use of laboratory monkeys is also accompanied by serious challenges in disease prevention and control. Laboratory monkey populations carry or are susceptible to a wide variety of pathogens, including highly pathogenic zoonotic agents (1, 2).B virus is widely prevalent in monkey populations, typically presenting a benign course, yet it poses a significant threat to human health, potentially causing encephalomyelitis with a case fatality rate as high as 40% (3, 4); Mycobacterium tuberculosis (TB) is also a common pathogen in laboratory monkeys, particularly in Old World monkeys. Tuberculosis not only causes morbidity and mortality in monkey colonies, leading to substantial economic losses, but also represents a serious zoonotic disease that threatens public health security (5, 6). In recent years, with the frequent occurrence of global public health events, emerging or re-emerging zoonotic viruses such as monkeypox virus have garnered significant attention. Their transmission and surveillance in monkey populations are of critical importance (7, 8). In addition, infections with pathogens such as Simian Immunodeficiency Virus (SIV), simian measles virus, Toxoplasma gondii, and Chlamydia spp. are also common in laboratory monkey populations. These infections may manifest as overt diseases or remain in latent or subclinical states (9–12). Gastrointestinal parasites have also been documented in macaque populations, with potential zoonotic implications (13).The presence of infectious diseases in laboratory monkeys directly compromises their animal welfare and health, affecting the stability and breeding of the population. Latent infections with pathogens may serve as uncontrolled confounding variables in experimental studies, impairing the accuracy, reproducibility, and reliability of research outcomes. They may even lead to erroneous judgments regarding the safety and efficacy of drugs or therapies. Therefore, the establishment and application of accurate, rapid, and efficient veterinary diagnostic techniques play a critical role in the early detection, precise identification, and effective surveillance of infectious diseases in laboratory monkeys.Beyond single-pathogen threats, the epidemiological reality in laboratory monkey colonies is further complicated by frequent co-infections. Studies have shown that co-infection with TB and Simian Retrovirus (SRV) is prevalent in macaque colonies-with SRV seroprevalence reaching 19~50% in some breeding colonies and TB infection rates as high as 30~45% in endemic facilities. Such co-infections can profoundly impact disease progression, immune responses, and experimental outcomes (2, 9, 14). Concurrent infections with B virus and SIV have also been reported, with B virus seroprevalence reaching 80~90% in adult macaques. SIV infection rates varying from 5 to 40% depending on geographic origin and housing conditions (3, 15, 16). Furthermore, a single macaque can be asymptomatically infected with multiple pathogens simultaneously. For example, co-infection rates of SIV with measles virus or Toxoplasma gondii have been documented at 10~30% in certain colonies (9–12, 17). Such co-infections create a complex network of latent infections that acts as an uncontrolled variable in experimental studies, impairing accuracy and reproducibility, and potentially leading to erroneous judgments regarding the safety and efficacy of drugs or therapies. The high prevalence of co - infections underscores the urgent need for diagnostic techniques capable of high - throughput, multiplex detection (18, 19).Previous reviews have addressed specific aspects of NHP diagnostics: Ohta focused on pathology (2), Yang et al. on viral detection (1), and Wolf et al. on TB testing (20). However, no previous review has integrated all four major diagnostic modalities within a single framework tailored specifically to laboratory monkeys. This Mini Review fills this gap by providing a comprehensive comparative overview across molecular, immunological, imaging, and traditional microbiological methods, clarifying scenario-specific suitability, identifying practical bottlenecks, and discussing emerging technologies. This work serves as a practical reference for veterinarians and researchers working with NHP models.The diagnosis of infectious diseases in laboratory monkeys carries significant biosafety and occupational health implications that must be carefully addressed. Specimen collection (e.g., blood, saliva, BALF, tissues) should be performed using appropriate restraint and sedation to minimize stress and injury risk. Specimen handling and transport must follow strict biosafety protocols to prevent aerosol generation, spills, and contamination. Containment measures-including biosafety cabinets, sealed centrifuges, and appropriate facility BSL levels-are essential when processing potentially infectious samples. Personal protective measures (e.g., gloves, gowns, face shields, N95 respirators) should be mandatory for all personnel handling monkey-derived specimens or performing necropsies. Decontamination of surfaces, equipment, and waste is critical to prevent environmental contamination. Occupational exposure management-including post-exposure prophylaxis for B virus, TB screening, and incident reporting systems-should be in place for all facilities housing laboratory monkeys (3). The integration of veterinary diagnostics with occupational-health monitoring ensures that diagnostic results from animals inform human health surveillance, creating a bidirectional safety net.These biosafety and occupational health considerations firmly embed laboratory-monkey diagnostics within the One Health framework. Robust diagnostic practices protect not only animal welfare by enabling early detection and treatment, but also occupational health by safeguarding facility personnel from zoonotic infections. They contribute to zoonotic disease prevention by identifying infected animals before transmission occurs, and to biosafety and biosecurity by containing pathogens at their source. Furthermore, accurate diagnostics enhance public-health surveillance for emerging zoonotic threats and ensure the reliability of biomedical research by maintaining specific-pathogen-free colonies and preventing undetected infections from confounding experimental data. Thus, veterinary diagnostics for laboratory monkeys represent a critical interface between animal and human health, embodying the core principles of One Health (21).To clearly demonstrate the novelty of this Mini Review, a structured comparison with previous reviews is warranted. Ohta (2) provided a comprehensive summary of pathologic characteristics of infectious diseases in macaques, with a focus on histopathological findings rather than diagnostic methodologies. Yang et al. (1) updated practices for viral detection in breeding macaques, primarily emphasizing molecular assays for specific viruses without coverage of other pathogen categories or non-molecular techniques. Wolf et al. (20) reviewed noninvasive testing strategies for tuberculosis detection in primates, but did not extend to other bacterial, viral, or parasitic pathogens. analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 免疫层析技术,如胶体金试纸条和免疫测定梳,因其简便性和无需设备的特点,在现场快速筛查中发挥重要作用(27)。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 首先,迫切需要进行前瞻性验证研究,采用标准化协议和明确的参考标准,以在真实世界条件下建立新诊断平台的真实性能。
analysis_zh.methods: 在多项研究中,qPCR对B病毒检测表现出100%的敏感性和100%的特异性,数字PCR(dPCR)对猴痘病毒的检测限低至45 copies/ml;基于CRISPR/Cas的检测方法在临床验证队列研究中也表现出100%的敏感性和100%的特异性。
analysis_zh.main_results: B病毒与SIV的并发感染也已被报道,其中B病毒血清流行率在成年猕猴中达到80~90%。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 它们正逐渐被新型免疫学方法如ELISA(23)所取代。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 它们通过在传播发生前识别感染动物,有助于人兽共患病的预防,并通过在源头控制病原体,有助于生物安全和生物安保。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 此外,准确的诊断有助于应对新兴人兽共患病威胁的公共卫生监测,并通过维持无特定病原体的群体和防止未检测到的感染干扰实验数据,确保生物医学研究的可靠性。

papers.title: Seroprevalence of 17 pathogens from an integrated national serosurvey in Niue
papers.abstract: Integrated serosurveillance (ISS), using multiplex bead assays to measure antibodies to multiple pathogens, can provide insights into population immunity and pathogen exposure. We estimated seroprevalence for neglected tropical diseases (NTDs), arboviruses, vaccine-preventable diseases, and enteric protozoa in Niue through a cross-sectional survey embedded within a World Health Organization (WHO) STEPwise survey from 24 February to 4 April 2025. Dried blood spots from participants aged ≥ 3 years were tested for 26 pathogen-specific antibodies. Among 750 participants (median age 37 years; range 3–93; 53% female), NTD seroprevalence was low (0% for yaws [among 165 participants aged ≤ 14 years] to 2.7% for cysticercosis). Arbovirus seroprevalence ranged from 3.1% (Zika) to 35.1% (dengue serotype 4). Dengue seropositivity increased with age ( p < 0.05). Measles and rubella seroprevalence exceeded 98%, while diphtheria and tetanus seropositivity was lower in older age groups ( p ≤ 0.03). Cryptosporidium seroprevalence (68.7%) increased with age ( p < 0.001), while Giardia seroprevalence was low (4.1%). Findings demonstrate the utility of ISS to generate policy-relevant surveillance data, although interpretation is limited by the cross-sectional design and non-probability sampling.

papers.title: Evaluation of Vaccination Coverage and Compliance Among Medical Students: A Cross-Sectional Documentary Analysis
papers.abstract: Introduction: Vaccination is a cornerstone of primary healthcare, particularly critical for medical students and healthcare professionals due to constant occupational exposure to infectious agents.This study aimed to evaluate the vaccination status of medical students at a private higher education institution in the Federal District, Brazil, comparing their self-perceived protection with actual immunization records.Methods: A cross-sectional, descriptive study was conducted between August 2024 and July 2025, involving 90 medical students from various semesters.Data collection utilized structured online questionnaires and documentary analysis of digital vaccination cards submitted via the "Meu SUS Digital" platform or physical records.Evaluated immunizations included hepatitis A, hepatitis B (HBV), measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR), tetanus/dT, yellow fever, meningococcal C and ACWY, influenza (2024 campaign), and COVID-19.Data were analyzed using absolute and relative frequencies.Results: Although 75 (83.3%)participants self-reported having an up-to-date vaccination card and 85 (94.4%) felt protected for clinical practice, documentary analysis revealed severe gaps.Only 16 (19.3%)participants possessed a completely up-to-date occupational schedule for all analyzed immunogens.Significant deficits included 56 (67.5%) lacking hepatitis A doses, 77 (92.8%) lacking meningococcal ACWY records, and 22 (26.5%)lacking the 2024 influenza vaccine.The primary reasons cited for missing vaccines were lack of availability at the appropriate age (n = 10, 43.5%) and unknown causes (n = 10, 43.5%).Descriptively, students with parents in the healthcare field and those in advanced internship semesters showed proportionally higher completeness rates, although overall coverage remained insufficient.Furthermore, 57 (63.3%) respondents recognized a lack of information regarding occupational infection risks during their academic training.Conclusions: A profound discrepancy exists between medical students' perceived immunological protection and their actual immunization status.These findings highlight an urgent need for institutional interventions, curriculum enhancements, and mandatory vaccination verification protocols to safeguard students and patients in clinical learning environments.
