papers.full_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing healthcare, with growing relevance in infectious diseases and clinical microbiology. This review summarizes current applications of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and large language models (LLMs) in these areas while critically evaluating their strengths and limitations. Although AI has shown promising performance in image analysis, molecular diagnostics, risk prediction, and clinical decision support, its routine implementation remains constrained by limited external validation, heterogeneous datasets, algorithmic bias, and challenges in generalizability and explainability. The review also discusses AI’s emerging role in scientific writing and the ethical and practical considerations associated with its clinical adoption. Overall, current evidence suggests that AI should be regarded as a complementary decision-support technology whose safe and effective integration depends on rigorous validation, high-quality data, and appropriate clinical oversight. The Dawn of Artificial Intelligence in HealthcareArtificial intelligence (AI) is a branch of computer science that develops computational systems capable of performing tasks that typically require human intelligence, including pattern recognition, prediction, and decision support. Artificial intelligence has become increasingly integrated into healthcare, offering new opportunities to improve diagnostics, prognostic assessment, and clinical decision-making. Recent advances in machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and large language models (LLMs), together with the increasing availability of digital health data, have accelerated the development of AI applications across medicine (1).In infectious diseases and clinical microbiology (IDCM), AI has attracted growing interest because it can improve laboratory diagnostics, antimicrobial stewardship, prognostic assessment, outbreak surveillance, and clinical decision support. Although numerous studies have reported promising results, important challenges related to external validation, data quality, model generalizability, and clinical implementation continue to limit the routine adoption of these technologies.This review was prepared based on the thematic discussions, expert presentations, and literature evaluations conducted within the 2025 Basic Education Program of the Assistants and Young Specialists Commission of the Turkish Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases, entitled AI in Infectious Diseases and Clinical Microbiology. Building on these educational activities, this review critically synthesizes current evidence on AI applications in IDCM, highlighting both their clinical potential and the methodological, practical, and ethical challenges that must be addressed before widespread implementation. The Role of AI in MedicineAI in medicine has evolved from early rule-based expert systems to modern ML and DL models capable of analyzing complex clinical data (2, 3). These approaches have been widely adopted in specialties such as radiology and pathology, where image-based analysis has demonstrated substantial clinical utility (4, 5). In contrast, AI applications in IDCM remain at an earlier stage of implementation because they require integrating microbiological, clinical, and epidemiological information. Accordingly, AI systems in this field should be evaluated according to their specific clinical applications, evidence base, and limitations rather than as a single technology. ML and DL in Infectious Diseases and Clinical MicrobiologyMachine learning and DL applications in IDCM have expanded rapidly over the past decade, driven by advances in computational methods and the increasing availability of digital laboratory and clinical data. Current applications can be broadly categorized into four major areas: diagnostic automation, clinical decision support, clinical documentation and symptom assessment, and epidemiological surveillance (Table 1). Although numerous studies have demonstrated promising results, most AI systems remain task-specific and have not yet undergone sufficient prospective or multicenter validation for routine clinical implementation.Table 1.Classification of general clinical AI tools relevant to IDCM practice. Category Representative tools and systems Clinical application in infectious diseases CDSSIBM Watson (Merative), Isabel Healthcare, DXplain, VisualDx, Sepsis Watch, Bayesian HealthDifferential diagnosis of rare conditions, sepsis risk prediction, and providing actionable clinical guidance.Symptom analyzersAda Health, Symptoma, Infermedica, Healthily, DxGPT (GPT-4)Analysis of patient-reported symptoms for triage, rare disease identification, and mobile health integration.Documentation and EHR systemsSuki AI, Nabla, Nuance DAX, DeepScribe, Epic Systems, Oracle CernerAutomated clinical note generation, ICD-10 coding, sepsis monitoring, and complication prediction within EHRs.Dermatological diagnosticsSkinive.MD, VisualDxClassification of exanthematous lesions (e.g., mpox, varicella, measles) using CNNs.Molecular and genomic AIDeepARG, PathoFact, PARGT, Nextstrain, PangolinAMR gene prediction and real-time viral mutation visualization for epidemiological surveillance.AI: Artificial intelligence, AMR: Antimicrobial resistance, CNNs: Convolutional neural networks, CDSS: Clinical decision support systems, EHRs: Electronic health records, ICD-10: International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision. Diagnostic Automation and Molecular Analysis Diagnostic microbiology is among the most suitable areas for AI implementation because many laboratory procedures involve repetitive image interpretation and pattern-recognition tasks. Deep learning models, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have demonstrated high diagnostic performance in automated Gram stain interpretation and digital culture plate analysis, with reported agreement rates exceeding 95% under controlled experimental conditions (6). Nevertheless, further validation in diverse laboratory settings is required before widespread implementation.Artificial intelligence has also advanced molecular diagnostics through automated analysis of whole-genome sequencing data. ML-based platforms, such as DeepARG and PARGT, enable rapid identification of antimicrobial resistance genes and facilitate genomic surveillance (7, 8). However, their performance remains dependent on sequencing quality, reference database completeness, and the continuous updating of resistance gene repositories. Clinical Decision Support Systems Clinical decision support systems (CDSS) integrate laboratory findings with clinical information to assist with diagnosis, risk prediction, and treatment decisions. AI-based sepsis prediction models, including Sepsis Watch and the Epic Sepsis Prediction Model (Epic Systems, Verona, WI, USA) and Epic’s Sepsis Prediction Model, have demonstrated the potential to identify patients at increased risk before clinical deterioration occurs (9). However, inconsistent performance across institutions, false-positive alerts, and alert fatigue remain important barriers to routine implementation.Similarly, AI-assisted diagnostic support platforms combine clinical findings with large medical knowledge bases to facilitate differential diagnosis, whereas natural language processing (NLP)-based applications improve access to evidence-based recommendations and clinical guidelines (10, 11). Although these tools may improve efficiency, they should be regarded as supportive technologies rather than autonomous diagnostic systems. Symptom Analyzers, Triage, and Documentation Recent advances in NLP and LLMs have expanded AI applications to symptom assessment and clinical documentation. Symptom analyzers may assist with preliminary patient triage, whereas AI-powered documentation systems can automatically generate clinical notes and reduce administrative workload (12-15). Despite these advantages, current LLM-based applications remain susceptible to hallucinations, incomplete contextual understanding, and variable performance across different clinical scenarios, emphasizing the need for careful clinician review. Epidemiological Surveillance and Real-World Performance Artificial intelligence has become an increasingly valuable tool for infectious disease surveillance by supporting genomic epidemiology, outbreak monitoring, and pathogen evolution analysis. Platforms such as Nextstrain have played an important role in monitoring viral evolution during the COVID-19 pandemic (16, 17). At the same time, the pandemic highlighted the importance of representative datasets, continuous model updating, and external validation, demonstrating that algorithmic performance alone does not guarantee successful implementation in real-world public health settings (18-20). From Microscope to AI: Current Evidence on AI Models in Medical ParasitologyMicroscopic diagnosis remains the cornerstone of medical parasitology but is often labor-intensive and dependent on experienced personnel. Consequently, AI-based image analysis has emerged as a promising approach to improve diagnostic efficiency and standardization, particularly in settings with limited access to expert microscopists (21).Current evidence is strongest for blood-borne parasites, particularly Plasmodium spp., where CNN-based models have consistently demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy under experimental conditions (22, 23). Similar automated ML frameworks are being developed to identify intestinal parasites in stool samples. For instance, DL algorithms trained on large datasets of helminth eggs have shown significant potential to differentiate species with high morphological similarity, such as Ascaris lumbricoides and Trichuris trichiura (24).More recently, multimodal LLMs, including GPT-4 and Gemini, have been explored for parasitological image interpretation. However, unlike CNN-based models specifically trained for image classification, these general-purpose systems have shown inconsistent performance in recognizing complex microscopic structures and remain susceptible to hallucinations, particularly when image quality or contextual information is limited (25).Recent literature largely agrees that while advanced computational models offer promising support for education and second-opinion assessment, they cannot yet function as primary diagnostic tools in parasitology. Therefore, current evidence supports using AI as an adjunct to, rather than a replacement for, expert microscopic evaluation, particularly in diagnostically challenging cases (26). DL in the Diagnosis of Exanthematous Infectious DiseasesDeep learning has been increasingly investigated for automated recognition of infectious skin diseases because visual lesion assessment is an important component of clinical diagnosis. Most studies have focused on CNN-based image classification models that can distinguish common exanthematous infections from non-infectious skin disorders (27, 28).Recent studies have explored CNN-based models for classifying infectious skin diseases, including mpox, Lyme disease, and measles (29-32). While these studies report promising diagnostic performance in controlled experimental settings, their generalizability to real-world clinical environments remains uncertain and requires further validation (33).Deep learning-supported systems also hold potential in dermatology by improving diagnostic consistency in atypical presentations and supporting remote evaluation through teledermatology applications (34). However, these systems’ performance depends heavily on the quality, representativeness, and diversity of training datasets. A major limitation is algorithmic bias, particularly the underrepresentation of darker skin tones in publicly available datasets, which may reduce diagnostic accuracy across diverse populations (35, 36).In addition, many current DL models rely exclusively on visual inputs and do not incorporate critical clinical information such as associated symptoms (e.g., fever, pruritus) or disease course, which are essential for differentiating infectious exanthems from non-infectious conditions such as drug eruptions.Several commercially available mobile applications provide AI-assisted assessment of skin lesions; however, they should be regarded as screening tools rather than diagnostic systems because performance varies by image quality, lesion characteristics, and patient population (35, 36).Future research should prioritize prospective multicenter validation and the integration of clinical, epidemiological, and imaging data to improve the robustness and clinical applicability of AI models for infectious skin diseases. AI-Based Antimicrobial ManagementAntimicrobial stewardship (AMS) is one of the most promising applications of AI in infectious diseases because it requires the integration of microbiological, clinical, and epidemiological data to support timely treatment decisions. Current AI applications focus primarily on optimizing empirical antibiotic selection, identifying patients at increased risk of resistant infections, and supporting antimicrobial prescribing through CDSS (37, 38).ML models, particularly those analyzing longitudinal electronic health record data, have demonstrated encouraging performance in predicting healthcare-associated infections and identifying patients at high risk of multidrug-resistant organism (MDRO) infections, including carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) (39, 40). These models may enable earlier risk stratification than conventional clinical scoring systems and support more targeted empirical antimicrobial therapy. However, most available evidence originates from retrospective studies, and prospective validation across different healthcare settings remains limited.Although DL models can identify complex relationships within large clinical datasets, their predictions are often difficult to interpret in routine clinical practice. Explainable AI (XAI) approaches may help clinicians understand which variables contribute most to model predictions and thereby improve confidence in AI-assisted recommendations. However, XAI does not provide complete transparency into the internal processes of complex models and should not be interpreted as establishing causal relationships (41-43).Large language models have recently emerged as potential AMS tools by summarizing clinical guidelines, assisting with literature retrieval, and supporting educational activities. Nevertheless, current LLMs remain susceptible to hallucinations, outdated knowledge, and limited access to real-time patient-specific information, limiting their use for independent therapeutic decision-making (44, 45).Overall, current evidence suggests that AI has considerable potential to optimize AMS by improving risk prediction and supporting antimicrobial prescribing. However, despite encouraging predictive performance, robust evidence demonstrating improvements in prescribing quality, antimicrobial consumption, or patient outcomes remains limited. Future progress will depend on high-quality clinical data, rigorous external validation, and successful integration of AI tools into AMS programs and routine clinical workflows (46). ML Applications in Predicting the Prognosis of Infectious DiseasesPredicting disease progression is one of the most promising AI applications in infectious diseases because timely risk stratification can improve patient management and resource allocation. Unlike diagnostic models, prognostic models aim to estimate future clinical outcomes by integrating clinical, laboratory, and increasingly multi-omics data. Recent advances in multi-omics technologies have enabled the integration of genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and conventional clinical data into ML-based prognostic models, supporting more individualized risk prediction (47, 48).Machine learning algorithms, including Random Forest, Support Vector Machines (SVM), and gradient boosting methods such as XGBoost, have been applied to predict outcomes in sepsis, COVID-19, and Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF) by integrating clinical and molecular data (47-50). For instance, in targeted metabolomic analyses of patients with CCHF, ML models have been used to analyze amino acid profiles, enabling the prediction of intensive care requirements with high reported accuracy. In parallel, specialized computational frameworks have facilitated biomarker discovery using transcriptomic and metabolomic datasets, expanding opportunities for precision prognostic modeling (50).Despite these encouraging findings, most prognostic models have been developed using retrospective datasets and lack prospective external validation. Challenges related to data imbalance, heterogeneous patient populations, and differences in clinical practice continue to limit model generalizability. Future studies should prioritize multicenter validation, standardized reporting, and assessment of clinical impact to determine whether improved predictive performance translates into better patient outcomes. AI in Scientific Writing and Scholarly PublishingArtificial intelligence is increasingly incorporated into the research and publication process, supporting activities ranging from literature retrieval and evidence synthesis to manuscript preparation and editorial screening. Unlike clinical decision-support applications, these tools primarily aim to improve research efficiency rather than generate new scientific evidence. Their growing adoption has also raised important questions regarding transparency, accountability, and responsible use. full_text_sections.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing healthcare, with growing relevance in infectious diseases and clinical microbiology. This review summarizes current applications of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and large language models (LLMs) in these areas while critically evaluating their strengths and limitations. Although AI has shown promising performance in image analysis, molecular diagnostics, risk prediction, and clinical decision support, its routine implementation remains constrained by limited external validation, heterogeneous datasets, algorithmic bias, and challenges in generalizability and explainability. The review also discusses AI’s emerging role in scientific writing and the ethical and practical considerations associated with its clinical adoption. Overall, current evidence suggests that AI should be regarded as a complementary decision-support technology whose safe and effective integration depends on rigorous validation, high-quality data, and appropriate clinical oversight.

analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 同时,专门的计算框架已促进了利用转录组和代谢组数据集进行生物标志物发现,扩展了精准预后建模的机会(50)。尽管有这些令人鼓舞的发现,大多数预后模型都是使用回顾性数据集开发的,并缺乏前瞻性外部验证。
analysis_zh.methods: 然而,其性能仍依赖于测序质量、参考数据库的完整性以及抗药性基因库的持续更新。

papers.full_text: 593 Commentary EMHJ – Vol. 32 No. 9 – 2026 Sudan's unprecedented conflict places its health system on the brink Damilare M Akintunde1,2, Arwa Mohamed1–3, Faisal Hamad1,4, Moayad MO Ahmed1,5, Sarah AY Adam1,6 and Rawa Badri1,7 1Research and Development, End the Neglect Initiative, Khartoum, Sudan. 2Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria, Nigeria (Correspondence to Damilare Akintunde: micdam2090@gmail.com). 3Family Medicine Council, Sudan Medical Specialization Board, Sudan. 4Faculty of Epidemiology and Population Health, London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, London, England, United Kingdom. 5Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences, Kassala University, Kassala, Sudan. 6Faculty of Medicine, University of Bahri, Khartoum, Sudan. 7Mycetoma Research Centre, University of Khartoum, Khartoum, Sudan. Keywords: health system, health care, health infrastructure, health access, conflict, resilience, supply chain, Sudan Citation: Akintunde DM, Mohamed A, Hamad F, Ahmed MMO, Adam SAY, Badri R. Sudan's unprecedented conflict places its health system on the brink. East Mediterr Health J. 2026;32(9):593–595. https://doi.org/10.26719/2026.32.9.593 Received: 05/02/2026; Accepted: 31/03/2026 Copyright © Authors 2026; Licensee: World Health Organization. EMHJ is an open-access journal. This paper is available under the Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial ShareAlike 3.0 IGO licence (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/3.0/igo). Introduction For more than 1000 days, the armed conflict that began in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces has profoundly disrupted health care nationally. Between April 2023 and June 2024, an estimated 26 000 deaths occurred in Khartoum State alone due to intentional injury-related causes, indicating the high levels of brutality in this densely populated area (1). There have been reports of physical injuries and disabilities with mental health consequences, in addition to rape and other forms of sexual violence, with approximately 6.9 million women and girls, and an increasing number of men and boys, at risk of gender- based violence (GBV) (2). The prolonged siege has triggered acute food insecurity and mass displacement has placed severe strains on livelihoods and deepened financial insecurity (2). The high levels of malnutrition, frequent disease outbreaks and worsening outcomes for individuals living with chronic conditions have resulted in increased morbidity and mortality. Maternal and neonatal deaths have increased markedly, alongside the increasing threat of antimicrobial resistance (2). Sudan’s health system is experiencing extreme dysfunction. Within 6 months from the onset of the war, nearly two-thirds of hospitals and medical centres had ceased operations (3). Looting of health facilities and medical supply stores has disrupted service delivery and created a critical shortage of essential medicines. These issues are further exacerbated by violence against health workers and a severe workforce shortage (3). Consequently, disease surveillance and health service delivery coordination have been significantly disrupted, with significant deterioration in availability, accessibility and quality of health care service nationwide (2,3). This commentary adds to existing evidence by highlighting the current state of Sudan’s health system amidst ongoing conflict, including its implications for the region, the urgency of required intervention, and actionable recommendations for the Sudanese Ministry of Health, World Health Organization and other partners. Health system collapse In conflict-affected areas, health facilities are compelled to shut down as a result of multiple intersecting factors, including persistent insecurity, looting, damage of medical infrastructure, severe shortage of health personnel, and difficulties in obtaining essential medical supplies (4). For example, in war-affected regions where ambulances are looted, communities are forced to rely on donkey carts and wheelbarrows as improvised means of transporting patients. Sudan’s pharmaceutical sector has largely ceased production of essential medicines, including antibiotics and established pharmaceutical distribution networks have been seriously disrupted, resulting in medication shortage and increased costs for pharmacies and patients (5). Targeted damage to telecommunications and health information infrastructure, together with attacks on health workers, has severely undermined the country’s health information systems. These deliberate disruptions have significantly impacted the ability to collect and transmit data, affecting the development of essential health system baseline data (4). In addition to injuries caused by the conflict, Sudan is witnessing extensive cases of infections, which are causing a health crisis. Cholera, malaria, measles, polio, and dengue fever infections have increased markedly, with more than 120 000 confirmed cholera cases alone responsible for more than 3000 deaths (6). Humanitarian efforts to address these constraints have achieved limited success, partly due to the shortage of personnel in coordination roles and insufficient presence at the state level. These challenges, compounded by inadequate funding and limited political pressure on the warring parties to comply with international humanitarian law and permit access, have resulted in the humanitarian response reaching only a small fraction of those in need (7). Implications for the region Sudan’s war has triggered the largest displacement crisis worldwide, with more than 14.5 million displaced— over 10.5 million inside the country and approximately 594 Commentary EMHJ – Vol. 32 No. 9 – 2026 4 million across borders into neighbouring countries, including Central African Republic, Chad, Egypt, Ethiopia, Libya, and South Sudan (8). As of September 2023, Chad alone had received more than 420 000 refugees, with crude mortality rates up to 20 times higher than before the conflict, due mainly to violence (9). These massive movements of people are placing overwhelming pressure on fragile health systems across the region. The effects on public health are not limited to Sudan; border-crossing by refugees has increased the risk of infectious disease transmission. The malaria, cholera and measles outbreaks have been fuelled by overcrowded camps with poor sanitation, interrupted vaccination programmes and limited medical services (10). As of March 2025, only 14% of hospitals and 16% of primary care facilities were still operating in Sudan, due to the worst conflict-driven humanitarian crisis in the world (11). The country's capacity to identify, stop and handle epidemics has been seriously compromised. These regional realities underscore the urgent need for coordinated cross-border health strategies. International cooperation is required to improve camp conditions, resume immunisation programmes, restore health care, and strengthen cross-border disease surveillance (10). Sudan’s unfolding health emergency is no longer confined within its boundaries; without collective action, it will continue to reverberate across the region, jeopardizing disease control and stretching humanitarian systems in multiple countries (9). Urgent priorities The destruction of infrastructure, mass displacement and increasing disease burdens are causing preventable morbidity and mortality. There is an urgent need to scale- up humanitarian assistance (4). Immediate priorities include maintaining access to health services using multiple approaches such as the use of mobile clinics, rebuilding health facilities at all levels of care, ensuring the protection of health care from attacks, and providing logistic support to guarantee a continuous flow of medical supplies (13). Sustained funding and operational support, alongside community empowerment and support to locally led initiatives (13), are critical to preserve life- saving capacity for immediate relief and long-term health system resilience. Supporting public health campaigns and community-based health promotions, including among displaced populations, could prevent disease outbreaks while improving access to available health care services (11). Expanding the cross-border health corridors would make services accessible to populations that have become inaccessible due to displacement, particularly along the borders with South Sudan and Chad, where the collapse of surveillance and referral networks have disrupted care and made people more susceptible to epidemics (11). WHO-led regional coordination efforts, in cooperation with relevant ministries of health, may facilitate the establishment of common surveillance channels, mobilisation of emergency response teams and coordination of health services where domestic efforts have failed. For example, opening the Adre Border crossing between Chad and Sudan is considered essential to enable the delivery of lifesaving humanitarian assistance (14). Evidence-based, effective and sustainable interven­ tions in conflict-affected settings in Ethiopia, Lebanon, South Africa, and Syria have shown that effective health response in conflict settings are dependent on strong governance, community involvement, capacity building, and integrated multisectoral strategies (4). Humanitarian and development organizations, in collaboration with the WHO, should support capacity-building of local authori­ ties and strengthening of local governance. The Ministry of Health and local actors should be supported to lead and help coordinate response, ensuring stronger local capac­ ity for recovery. To improve outbreaks control the Ministry of Health, with technical and logistics support from WHO and partners, should deploy rapid response teams to help restore surveillance and early warning systems, and stabilise supply chains, and support security for health workers. Donor-enabled interventions should extend beyond emergency aid to ensuring that the crisis does not evolve into a broader regional public health emergency (13). Conclusion Sudan is facing a severe humanitarian crisis characterised by conflict, displacement, mass casualties, and multiple disease outbreaks, compounded by the crippling of the health system. There is an urgent need to scale-up humanitarian efforts to improve access to health services at all levels and across care cascades, including curative and community-based preventive services, to ensure the delivery of immediate relief and increase resilience of the health system. The prolonged siege has triggered acute food insecurity and mass displacement has placed severe strains on livelihoods and deepened financial insecurity (2). The high levels of malnutrition, frequent disease outbreaks and worsening outcomes for individuals living with chronic conditions have resulted in increased morbidity and mortality. Maternal and neonatal deaths have increased markedly, alongside the increasing threat of antimicrobial resistance (2). Sudan’s health system is experiencing extreme dysfunction. Within 6 months from the onset of the war, nearly two-thirds of hospitals and medical centres had ceased operations (3). Looting of health facilities and medical supply stores has disrupted service delivery and created a critical shortage of essential medicines. These issues are further exacerbated by violence against health workers and a severe workforce shortage (3). Consequently, disease surveillance and health service delivery coordination have been significantly disrupted, with significant deterioration in availability, accessibility and quality of health care service nationwide (2,3). This commentary adds to existing evidence by highlighting the current state of Sudan’s health system amidst ongoing conflict, including its implications for the region, the urgency of required intervention, and actionable recommendations for the Sudanese Ministry of Health, World Health Organization and other partners. analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 据估计,仅在2023年4月至2024年6月期间,苏丹西达尔富尔州的难民和返乡人员中因故意伤害导致的死亡人数就达到了26 000人,表明该地区暴力程度极高(1)。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 这些问题进一步因对卫生工作者的暴力行为和严重的人力资源短缺而加剧(3)。
analysis_zh.methods: 苏丹西达尔富尔州难民和返乡人员在2023年抵达乍得时的高发病率和暴力情况:三项回顾性调查的结果。
analysis_zh.main_results: 霍乱、疟疾、[未提供术语]、脊髓灰质炎和登革热感染显著增加,仅霍乱确诊病例就超过120 000例,导致超过3000人死亡(6)。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 结论 苏丹正面临严重的卫生人道主义危机,其特征是冲突、人口流离失所、大量伤亡以及多种疾病的暴发,同时卫生系统也受到严重削弱。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 公共卫生状况分析,2025年3月10日。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 截至2025年3月,由于全球最严重的冲突引发的人道主义危机,苏丹仅有14%的医院和16%的初级卫生保健设施仍在运营(11)。

papers.title: Determinants of Delayed and Missed Childhood Immunization Among Mothers Attending Primary Healthcare Centers in Al-Diwaniyah City, Iraq: A Cross-Sectional Study
papers.abstract: Background: Childhood immunization is a cost-effective public health intervention; however, delayed and missed vaccinations remain significant challenges. This study aimed to determine the prevalence and key determinants of childhood immunization non-compliance among mothers attending primary healthcare centers (PHCs). Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among 300 mothers of children aged 0–24 months attending PHCs. Data were collected using structured, interviewer-administered questionnaires and verified through immunization cards. Non-compliance was defined as a delay of ≥4 weeks beyond the scheduled date or omission of a due vaccine dose. Binary logistic regression was performed using SPSS version 26 to identify independent predictors. Results: Immunization non-compliance was observed in 49.7% of children (n=149). The highest non-compliance rates were reported for IPV (35.7%), measles-rubella vaccine (34.3%), and the third dose of pentavalent vaccine (25.3%). Major barriers included child illness on vaccination day (45.0%), caregiver forgetfulness (38.9%), and fear of adverse effects (32.9%). ; ; M; Primary healthcare; Vaccine hesitancy; Immunization barriers; Cross-sectional study.
papers.journal: UPI Journal of Pharmaceutical Medical and Health Sciences

analysis.study_design_and_population: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among 300 mothers of children aged 0–24 months attending primary healthcare centers.
analysis.methods: Data were collected using structured, interviewer-administered questionnaires and verified through immunization cards. analysis.summary_en: This cross-sectional study examines the prevalence and determinants of childhood immunization non-compliance among mothers in Al-Diwaniyah City, Iraq. The research highlights that 49.7% of children experienced delayed or missed vaccinations, with the highest rates observed for measles-rubella vaccine (34.3%), IPV (35.7%), and the third dose of pentavalent vaccine (25.3%). The study identifies key barriers such as child illness, caregiver forgetfulness, and fear of adverse effects. While the findings provide insights into vaccine hesitancy and immunization barriers, the study's single-city focus and reliance on self-reported data limit its generalizability. The results suggest the need for targeted interventions to improve immunization compliance, particularly for measles-related vaccines.

Therapeutic potential of oncolytic viruses in hematopoietic malignancies: from preclinical insights to clinical realities

papers.full_text: While certain forms of lymphoma—such as classical Hodgkin lymphoma—are classified as curable, with over half of all patients achieving remission following first-line therapy, a significant proportion of patients still suffer from relapsed or refractory disease. Through autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy can significantly improve survival rates, their widespread clinical utility is constrained by logistical bottlenecks, manufacturing complexities, and high financial burdens. Similarly, antibody-drug conjugates and bispecific antibodies have achieved striking success against hematologic malignancies, but their clinical adoption is often hindered by the requirement for continuous infusion. Consequently, systemically delivered oncolytic viruses engineered to express immunotherapeutic elements have emerged as highly innovative alternatives. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the current landscape and outlines the therapeutic potential of oncolytic virotherapy in the fight against hematopoietic malignancies. We cross-examined a robust dataset of over 100 preclinical investigations to critically assess the therapeutic efficacy and safety profiles of more than ten diverse oncolytic virus platforms developed for blood cancer treatment, alongside multiple early-phase clinical trials that are completed or currently underway. By synthesizing these preclinical and clinical data, we propose three critical development pathways—enhancing target specificity, arming viral vectors, and designing synergistic combination regimens—to accelerate the translation of clinically viable oncolytic viruses for hematologic oncology. Introduction and methodologyOncolytic viruses (OVs) have been widely studied in solid tumors, typically through intratumoral administration. In contrast, hematopoietic malignancies—which inherently require systemic drug delivery rather than local injection—have historically received less attention as primary targets for OV therapy. In this review, we explored data from clinical applications and trials, tracing evidence back through preclinical and basic research. By analyzing the current landscape of utilizing OVs to treat hematopoietic malignancies, we highlight this systemic targeting paradigm as possessing a uniquely favorable therapeutic window for advanced OV research.This mini-review was conducted by searching the PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov databases up to July 2026 using the terms “oncolytic virus” and “hematopoietic malignancies” or “blood cancer” or “lymphoma” or “leukemia” or “multiple myeloma.” Additional references were identified through citation tracking of relevant reviews and primary studies, prioritizing the most recent and clinically significant trials, preclinical advances, and mechanistic insights.Inclusion criteria: Studies were included if they evaluated live oncolytic virus platforms specifically targeting hematopoietic malignancies, lymphomas, leukemias, or multiple myeloma in preclinical models or clinical trials. Only articles published in English were considered, with no restrictions applied to publication date or study type.Exclusion criteria: Non-English articles, abstract-only publications lacking primary data, and studies focusing strictly on solid tumors without hematological evaluations were excluded.Initial database searches yielded a combined pool of records. Duplicates were removed, and the remaining articles were screened by the first reviewer based on title and abstract. Full texts of potentially eligible studies were then independently assessed against the inclusion criteria by a second reviewer. Any discrepancies regarding article selection or data extraction were resolved through consensus discussion between both reviewers prior to final inclusion Supplementary Tables and Figure 1. For each eligible study, information regarding study design, disease indication, efficacy-related outcomes, safety profiles, and adverse events associated with oncolytic virotherapy was collected and summarized.Figure 1Pre-clinical and clinical studies using OVs to treat blood cancers. Pre-clinical and clinical studies using OVs to treat blood cancers recorded in the PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov databases in the past three decades are distributed according to the publication year (X-axis) and virus types (Y-axis). For preclinical studies, the numbers inside the blue circles indicate the number of studies conducted for each OV in that year; those without numbers indicate that only one study was conducted. The Pteropine orthoreovirus (Sikamat virus) grouped under ‘Other’ is a distinct bat-borne species and not the mammalian reovirus (pelareorep) shown as ‘Reovirus’. Detail information was collected in Supplementary Tables 1, 2, from which the figure was generated using Python (Matplotlib).Scatter plot showing years of publication for studies on various oncolytic viruses from 1995 to 2025. Blue circles represent pre-clinical studies, and red stars denote clinical studies or case reports. Each row corresponds to a different virus, including measles virus, adenovirus, vesicular stomatitis virus, reovirus, vaccinia virus, myxoma virus, Newcastle disease virus, herpes simplex virus, and others. Most clinical studies occur after 2015, with recent entries for SARS-CoV-2. A legend specifies the meaning of symbols. The start: clinical case reports of tumor regressions after virus infectionThe therapeutic potential of viruses in oncology was initially inferred from clinical observations of spontaneous tumor regression following naturally acquired viral infections. Notably, transient remissions in patients with leukemia and lymphoma were historically reported during concurrent influenza or measles virus (MV) infections. More recently, similar remissions have been documented in hematologic malignancies following severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection. The inherent tumor-selectivity demonstrated by many wild-type viruses is largely attributed to the altered cellular landscape of neoplastic cells. Specifically, the hallmarks of cancer create a permissive microenvironment that overlaps significantly with cellular features required for efficient viral replication. Oncolytic viruses: a new generation of live cancer cell killersOVs are replication-competent, biologically active agents that exert anti-cancer effects through two principal mechanisms: direct tumor cell lysis and indirect stimulation of systemic anti-tumor immunity. In hematologic malignancies, where cancer cells reside in immune-privileged niches such as the bone marrow or peripheral blood, this dual functionality is particularly advantageous. On one hand, OVs themselves exploit molecular vulnerabilities in malignant cells; on the other hand, OVs can be armed with immunomodulatory transgenes to amplify their therapeutic impact. Pre-clinical studies on evaluating therapeutic OVs in blood cancersTo comprehensively examine and summarize the existing literature regarding OVs in blood cancer therapy and explore treatment-related outcomes, we first retrieved citations using the terms indicated in the Methodology section. After the title and abstract screening phase, the non-overlapping research articles were combined and analyzed. Then we grouped these studies according to the different virus types. Among them, MV was the most frequently studied in publications, followed by adenovirus, vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) and reovirus (Figure 1 and Supplementary Table 1). Below, we will analyze the study setup and major outcomes of these studies based on different OV types.Although adenovirus was the most frequently applied one in clinical trials,1 only a handful of studies were performed in blood cancer treatment. These studies ranged from systematic evaluation to rational design of human adenoviruses for enhanced blood cancer therapy. In an earlier study by Qian and colleagues, E1B55K-deleted adenovirus type 5 (Ad5) armed with melanoma differentiation-associated gene-7/interleukin-24 (MDA-7/IL-24) was tested in a range of blood cancer cell lines. Although a potent anti-cancer effect was observed in vitro and in vivo, the effect was limited to Ad5 major receptor (coxsackievirus and adenovirus receptor)-expressing hematological malignancies (Qian et al., 2008). Follow-up studies solved the problem by using chimeric Ad35 fiber (Wang et al., 2009; Wenthe et al., 2020). Another study compared the growth-inhibition effect of adenovirus and herpes simplex virus (HSV) on several cell lines; HSV was more effective (Zhang et al., 2011). Realizing the limitation from Ad5, a broad range of human adenoviruses were evaluated by Barry’s research group. They observed robust killing and delayed lymphoma growth by species D adenoviruses (Chen et al., 2011). However, in mouse B cell lymphoma model A20, only prophylactic immunization by adenovirus against A20 tumors can protect against A20 lymphomas; established A20 tumors were not controlled by A20-expressing adenovirus immunization (Weaver et al., 2011). While OV alone is not enough to control blood malignancies, a combination approach highlights the optimized development strategy. A rationally designed OAd5F35, Ad5-based chimeric virus with Ad35 fiber, armed with TMZ-CD40L and 4-1BBL was evaluated in combination with CAR-T therapy. The fiber switch to Ad35 enabled the use of CD46, which is up-regulated in hematological malignancies, thereby enhancing targeting and replication. Interestingly, OAd5F35 infection induced transgene expression and a change in immune markers. In combination with CAR-T therapy, the infected lymphoma cells were found to secrete chemokines to attract CAR-T cells, thereby increased CAR-T cell activation was observed. Importantly, the enhanced lymphoma cell killing was also observed in vivo in xenograft models (Wenthe et al., 2021). Similarly, a CD47 antibody expressing adenovirus (Ad5-hTert-E1A-IRES-E1B with mCMV-mCD47nb-Fc) as in situ tumor vaccination also showed positive immune-regulation and protection from tumor re-challenge (Zhang et al., 2022). These data suggested that adenovirus alone is not enough to control such aggressive hematological malignancies; a combination approach should be the development strategy of choice.Talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC), based on HSV-1, is so far the only OV approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for the treatment of melanoma (Zhang T. et al., 2023). However, only a few studies have explored its potential in hematological malignancies. In the search for molecular indicators for permissiveness to HSV therapy, transcription factors downstream of Ras were evaluated in non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL) cell lines infected with R3616, an HSV-1 with a deletion of the viral γ134.5 gene. Ras signaling was assessed by immunoblotting for different downstream effectors, which revealed ERK/ELK as a suitable predictive indicator for selection of cancer cells with increased sensitivity to HSV-based therapy (Esfandyari et al., 2009). As G47Δ was approved in Japan in 2021 (Frampton, 2022), a similar version of this OV was evaluated in a broad panel of 26 cell lines and 15 primary cells derived from various lineages of hematological malignancies (Ishino et al., 2021). The expression of an HSV-1 receptor, nectin-1, was identified as a determining factor in the oncolytic effect determined by viral entry and cytotoxicity. Although only a low level of virus replication was detected in hematological cancer cells, the virus could induce immunogenic cell death and kill the malignant cells. Importantly, this study demonstrated that systemic tumor-specific CD8 + T cell responses efficiently concentrated at tumor sites, suggesting that local intratumoral injection of HSV-1 is expected to provoke effective immune responses even for systemic tumors such as hematological malignancies. Recently, an oncolytic type II HSV (oHSV2) was explored in the treatment of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) (Zhang J. et al., 2023). In comparison with the clinical chemotherapeutic drug doxorubicin (DOX), oHSV2 revealed a better therapeutic profile on the apoptotic, invasive, and proliferative capacity of DLBCL cells in vitro. Moreover, oHSV2 can also inhibit transplanted tumor growth and accelerate CD4 + T and CD8 + T cell infiltration in mice, with an acceptable safety profile in the organs of tumor-bearing animals. To explore the potential of combination therapy with immune-checkpoint inhibitors, this study also showed oHSV2 can inhibit the PD-1/PD-L1 immune-checkpoint, thereby restraining cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) apoptosis and encouraging CTL proliferation. The combination therapy resulted in enhanced killing of malignant cells and inhibited tumor growth in mice. Similar to the adenovirus studies, combination therapy and the individual receptor profile are essential for further HSV application in hematological malignancies.The rat protoparvovirus H-1 (H-1PV) does not infect or cause any disease in humans, but has natural tropism for human cancer cells. H-1PV demonstrates a broad range of anticancer activities in several preclinical cancer models and in clinical trials (Geletneky et al., 2017; Bretscher and Marchini, 2019; Hajda et al., 2021). The first study to apply H-1PV to Burkitt’s lymphoma (BL)-derived cell lines showed high sensitivity to H-1PV-induced oncolysis in vitro. The H-1PV infection of BL lines is productive and leads to predominantly necrotic cell death. Importantly, normal B cells from healthy donors are resistant to H-1PV infection (Angelova et al., 2009). Then a large panel of lymphoma- and leukemia-derived cell lines was included to assess the capacity of H-1PV to target hematological malignancies. This study revealed that most cell lines are sensitive to H-1PV-induced cell death, and the progeny virion production, rather than virus entry, was the determining factor. Among all tested cells, DLBCL cells supported high levels of H-1PV progeny virion production and were almost totally eradicated by very low virus doses. Moreover, DLBCL cell lines with upregulated expression of aldehyde dehydrogenase 1A1 conferring chemotherapy resistance were among the most sensitive H-1PV targets (Angelova et al., 2017). A recent study extended this work to cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL). H-1PV infects and induces oncolysis in both classically grown CTCL suspension cultures and in a novel, in vivo-relevant, heterotypic spheroid model, but not in healthy donor controls, including peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). In CTCL spheroid co-cultures with PBMCs, treatment with the virus increased infiltration of the spheroids with immune cells (Angelova et al., 2024).Among oncolytic platforms, MV is the most extensively studied in hematological malignancies, owing to its vaccine safety record and its natural tropism for CD46 and the lymphocyte receptor SLAM/CD150 (Ong et al., 2006; Engeland and Ungerechts, 2021). Vaccine-strain MV was found to regress human B-cell lymphoma xenografts even in the presence of anti-MV antibodies (Grote et al., 2001). Subsequent improvement in specificity was achieved by retargeting viral entry. Vectors retargeted to CD20, armed with a prodrug convertase, and combined with cyclophosphamide and fludarabine regressed mantle cell lymphoma xenografts, though with limited survival benefit (Bucheit et al., 2003; Ungerechts et al., 2010). Analogous CD30 and CD38 retargeting extended the approach to Hodgkin lymphoma and myeloma (Peng et al., 2003; Hanauer et al., 2018). Importantly, efficacy was tracked with receptor usage and innate signaling. For instance, SLAM-dependent entry in mantle cell lymphoma virotherapy, EBV-driven CD150 upregulation and type I interferon responsiveness have been shown to determine susceptibility, and Bcl-2 has been shown to slow oncolysis in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (Patel et al., 2011; Miest et al., 2013; Fernandez et al., 2014; Takeda et al., 2014). To facilitate systemic delivery in the face of anti-MV immunity, studies have shown that both carrier and mesenchymal stromal cells have the capacity to deliver the virus to sites of disseminated disease (Iankov et al., 2007; Castleton et al., 2014). In particular, the development of the thyroidal sodium iodide symporter-expressing MV-NIS has advanced MV into early-phase clinical testing for multiple myeloma (MM) (Dingli et al., 2004).Vaccinia virus (VV), a large-genome poxvirus that tolerates sizeable transgene insertions, has been used in blood cancers mainly as an arming and combination platform rather than as a bare oncolytic agent. An attenuated VV delivered by cytokine-induced killer cells trafficked to residual murine B-cell lymphoma and prevented relapse through acquired antitumor immunity (Contag et al., 2010). Its coding capacity has since carried both pro-apoptotic and immunomodulatory transgenes. Vectors co-expressing miR-34a and Smac have been shown to induce cell death in MM cells (Lei et al., 2016), and a VV-Beclin1 drove autophagic death of NHL cells, sensitizing them to R-CHOP immune-chemotherapy (Rituximab, Cyclophosphamide, Hydroxydaunomycin, Oncovin and Prednisone) (Xie et al., 2021). Notably, immune-arming constructs have been developed to combine oncolysis with a defined effector mechanism. A CD19 bispecific T-cell engager recruited T cells, an anti-CD47 nanobody reprogrammed macrophages, and interleukin-18 relieved T-cell exhaustion, each prolonging survival in lymphoma models (Lei et al., 2022; Li et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026). The natural adjuvant embelin further enhanced replication and antitumor immunity (Wang et al., 2020). With its large coding capacity and systemic deliverability, vaccinia is a flexible platform whose efficacy comes mainly from immune arming, not oncolysis alone.VSV, a non-human rhabdovirus highly sensitive to type I interferon…

papers.title_original: Therapeutic potential of oncolytic viruses in hematopoietic malignancies: from preclinical insights to clinical realities

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess the therapeutic potential of oncolytic viruses (OVs) in hematopoietic malignancies, addressing the limitations of current treatments like autologous stem cell transplantation and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy. The research sought to evaluate the efficacy and safety profiles of OVs targeting hematological cancers, including lymphomas, leukemias, and multiple myeloma, through preclinical and early-phase clinical trials.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A systematic review was conducted by searching PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov databases up to July 2026, using terms related to oncolytic viruses and hematopoietic malignancies. The study included preclinical models and clinical trials evaluating live OVs targeting hematological cancers, with a focus on recent and clinically significant trials and mechanistic insights.
analysis.methods: The review included a comprehensive analysis of over 100 preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials, evaluating various OVs such as adenovirus, measles virus, and herpes simplex virus (HSV). Methods involved assessing therapeutic efficacy and safety profiles, including immunogenic cell death, immune regulation, and combination therapies with checkpoint inhibitors.
analysis.main_results: The review found that OVs showed therapeutic potential in hematopoietic malignancies, with some studies demonstrating improved outcomes when combined with other therapies. For instance, HSV-1 showed better therapeutic profiles compared to doxorubicin in vitro, and measles virus was found to be highly sensitive to oncolysis in Burkitt’s lymphoma cell lines.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as indicating the potential of OVs in hematopoietic malignancies, particularly when combined with other therapies. Novel insights included the ability of OVs to induce immunogenic cell death and to enhance immune responses, suggesting a favorable therapeutic window for advanced OV research.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings could inform the development of new treatment strategies for hematopoietic malignancies, potentially improving patient outcomes and reducing the reliance on costly and logistically challenging therapies like CAR T-cell therapy.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the reliance on preclinical data and early-phase clinical trials, which may not fully represent the complexities of human disease. The evidence strength is moderate due to the variability in study designs and the need for further clinical validation.

analysis.summary_en: This review assessed the therapeutic potential of oncolytic viruses in hematopoietic malignancies, highlighting their efficacy and safety profiles in preclinical and early-phase clinical trials. The findings suggest potential improvements in treatment strategies for hematological cancers, particularly when combined with other therapies.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估溶瘤病毒(OVs)在血液恶性肿瘤中的治疗潜力,解决当前如自体干细胞移植和嵌合抗原受体(CAR)T细胞疗法等治疗手段的局限性。研究旨在通过预临床和早期临床试验评估OVs针对血液系统癌症(包括淋巴瘤、白血病和多发性骨髓瘤)的疗效和安全性。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本系统综述通过在PubMed和ClinicalTrials.gov数据库中使用与溶瘤病毒和血液恶性肿瘤相关的术语进行检索,截至2026年7月。研究包括了评估活OVs治疗血液系统癌症的预临床模型和临床试验,重点是最近和临床意义重大的试验和机制见解。
elements_zh.methods: 综述包括了对超过100项预临床研究和早期临床试验的全面分析,评估了腺病毒、麻疹病毒和单纯疱疹病毒(HSV)等多种OVs。方法包括评估治疗疗效和安全性,包括免疫细胞死亡、免疫调节和与检查点抑制剂的联合疗法。
elements_zh.main_results: 综述发现,OVs在血液恶性肿瘤中显示出治疗潜力,一些研究显示与其他疗法联合使用时可以改善结果。例如,HSV-1在体外显示了更好的治疗效果,而麻疹病毒在Burkitt淋巴瘤细胞系中对溶瘤作用高度敏感。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释了这些发现表明OVs在血液恶性肿瘤中的潜力,特别是在与其他疗法联合使用时。新颖的见解包括OVs能够诱导免疫细胞死亡并增强免疫应答,这表明高级OV研究具有有利的治疗窗口。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以为血液恶性肿瘤的新治疗策略提供信息,可能改善患者结果并减少对昂贵且物流复杂的CAR T细胞疗法的依赖。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 研究的局限性包括依赖于预临床数据和早期临床试验,这可能无法完全代表人类疾病的复杂性。证据强度中等,因为研究设计的差异性和需要进一步的临床验证。

papers.abstract_zh: 本综述提供了当前溶瘤病毒治疗在对抗血液恶性肿瘤方面的全面概述。在本综述中,我们探讨了临床应用和试验中的数据,追溯证据至预临床和基础研究。通过分析利用溶瘤病毒(OVs)治疗血液恶性肿瘤的现状,我们强调了这种全身靶向模式具有独特的有利治疗窗口,适合高级OV研究。本迷你综述通过在PubMed和ClinicalTrials.gov数据库中使用“溶瘤病毒”和“血液恶性肿瘤”或“血液癌症”或“淋巴瘤”或“白血病”或“多发性骨髓瘤”等术语进行检索,截至2026年7月。通过引用相关综述和原始研究的引用追踪,我们确定了额外的参考文献,优先考虑最近和临床意义重大的试验、预临床进展和机制见解。纳入标准:研究如果评估了专门针对血液恶性肿瘤、淋巴瘤、白血病或多发性骨髓瘤的活溶瘤病毒平台,则被纳入。尽管某些类型的淋巴瘤——如经典霍奇金淋巴瘤——被归类为可治愈的,超过一半的患者在接受一线治疗后达到缓解,但仍有相当一部分患者仍遭受复发或难治性疾病。通过自体干细胞移植(ASCT)和嵌合抗原受体(CAR)T细胞疗法可以显著提高生存率,但其临床应用受到物流瓶颈、制造复杂性和高昂的财务负担的限制。同样,抗体药物偶联物和双特异性抗体等治疗方法也存在类似的挑战。

Yes Not now Full Episodes Podcasts Newsletters Live Pennsylvania doctor urges vaccination as measles outbreak grows Oct 15, 2026 6:40 PM EDT By — Jackson Hudgins Jackson Hudgins By — Amna Nawaz Amna Nawaz Leave your feedback Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/pennsylvania-doctor-urges-vaccination-as-measles-outbreak-grows Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Transcript Audio The CDC has confirmed more than 4,000 cases of measles this year as the country grapples with the largest outbreak of the highly infectious virus in 35 years. Nearly a fifth of cases comprise children under the age of five, and 95% are among unvaccinated people. Amna Nawaz spoke with Dr. Evan Shirey, a pediatric infectious disease doctor based in Pennsylvania. Read the Full Transcript Notice: Transcripts are machine and human generated and lightly edited for accuracy. They may contain errors. Amna Nawaz: The CDC has now confirmed more than 4,000 cases of measles this year as the country grapples with the largest outbreak of the highly infectious virus in 35 years. Nearly a fifth of cases comprise children under the age of 5, and more than 90 percent are among people who are unvaccinated. Pennsylvania is the epicenter of the outbreak with more than 1, 100 cases. That includes five measles-related deaths and potentially a sixth still being investigated. For more on what we're seeing and its impact, we're joined now by Dr. Evan Shirey. He's a pediatric infectious disease doctor based in Hershey, Pennsylvania. Dr. Shirey, welcome and thanks for joining us. Dr. Evan Shirey, Penn State Health: Thank you for having me. Amna Nawaz: So you're in Hershey in Central Pennsylvania, the middle of your state's measles epicenter. Just tell us what you're seeing at your hospital right now. Dr. Evan Shirey: Yes, unfortunately, I have been seeing a lot of children and a lot of babies who have been admitted to our hospital and have been very sick. I am seeing the severe consequences that can come from this virus. Amna Nawaz: Tell us about those consequences. What are the measles like in those young children you're seeing? How does it present? Dr. Evan Shirey: So there are a number of complications that can come about from measles. One that we really worry about is encephalitis, and that's when the virus causes infection of the brain. Children with encephalitis from measles in some cases may be unresponsive. In other cases, they may be awake and aware, but confused. They don't know where they are. They're scared, in some cases, not even able to recognize their own parents. These cases are really, really tragic to see. We see infections where the virus infects the lungs or the airways, and we call that a bronchopneumonia. These children might come in breathing really fast, breathing really heavily, gasping for air, in some cases needing different forms of respiratory support and oxygen, and in some of the extreme cases we have seen have even need to be put on a ventilator. We have seen babies who have come in who are unable to nurse or unable to take bottles, and just all forms of various different kinds of suffering from the manifestations of these infections. Amna Nawaz: And, Dr. Shirey, do we know what's driving this outbreak, how it's gotten so severe in Pennsylvania? Dr. Evan Shirey: So we know that, historically, the measles virus caused a lot of infections. We had three or four million infections every single year in this country, and that also resulted in 50,000 hospitalizations, around 500 deaths every year. So we know this is really bad virus. We know the measles virus can spread like wildfire. It is famous for how infectious it is. One person with measles can infect up to 18 others. The reason that we have not been seeing measles cases up until now is because we had a very safe and a very effective vaccine that we had been using for decades that actually resulted in elimination of the virus from this country. The virus is back because of a failure to vaccinate. Amna Nawaz: Given that we thought measles was eliminated about 25 years ago, is this something you ever thought you would be seeing during your time practicing as a doctor? Dr. Evan Shirey: Absolutely not. I spent a lot of time learning about measles as a medical student and as a resident and as an infectious diseases fellow going through all of my training. I always expected that measles was going to stay in the textbooks, and I did not expect that I would live in a world where I was in an ICU taking care of patients in real life. Amna Nawaz: Can I ask you about the rhetoric we're hearing from some of the nation's leaders? I mean, famously, the HHS secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has had some anti-vaccine views and vaccine skepticism he's expressed. How does that complicate your job on the ground? Dr. Evan Shirey: I think it's a real shame. I think that this outbreak just really highlights how important it is that, when we communicate about these important health issues, that we lead with honesty and the truth. I think it's -- overall has been a shame that the anti-vaccine movement has gained the power that they have and that they have gained the influence in reaching ordinary Pennsylvanians. I see in my clinic when I talk to people about vaccines that the types of fears that people have over these last five, 10 years are really just a different dynamic from the way things used to be. And I think that is largely -- unfortunately, it's related to the success of the anti-vaccine movement as a whole. Amna Nawaz: Whenever we cover these kinds of stories, I should mention to you we hear from people who say, look, if you or your children are vaccinated, you will be fine, so there's not much to worry about. analysis.brief_en: A measles outbreak in the United States has reached its largest scale in 35 years, with the CDC confirming over 4,000 cases this year. Pennsylvania is the epicenter, reporting more than 1,100 cases, including five deaths and a potential sixth under investigation. The outbreak has disproportionately affected unvaccinated individuals, particularly children under five. Dr. Evan Shirey, a pediatric infectious disease doctor in Hershey, Pennsylvania, highlights the severe health consequences, such as encephalitis and bronchopneumonia, which have led to hospitalizations and, in some cases, the need for ventilator support. The outbreak is attributed to declining vaccination rates, and Shirey emphasizes the importance of vaccination to prevent further spread. The situation is being actively managed by healthcare professionals, but the exact cause of the outbreak and the status of the potential sixth death remain under investigation. The outbreak underscores the risks associated with vaccine hesitancy and the resurgence of a virus that was previously eliminated in the country.

analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: CDC已确认麻疹 暴发,医疗专业人员正在积极应对这一情况。暴发归因于对接种疫苗的犹豫不决,谢里尔博士敦促接种疫苗接种以防止进一步传播。暴发的确切原因和潜在第六例死亡病例仍在调查中。[N10,N18,N19,N21,N24,N25,N26,N27,N50,N52]

(Cynthia S. Goldsmith; William Bellini, Ph.D./Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/TNS/TNS) By David Mowery | dmowery@readingeagle.com | Reading Eagle PUBLISHED: October 16, 2026 at 4:36 PM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Berks County has added a confirmed measles case, bringing the total this year in the county to seven. The case was included in the state Department of Health’s latest update Friday that reported a total of 1,260 cases in 43 counties. The state continues to report five deaths, acknowledging that is investigating a recent death in Franklin County. The Franklin County coroner on Monday reported the measles-associated death of a 39-year-old woman on Oct. 11. State officials in their update said that to be considered measles-associated, the department’s epidemiological definition must meet the following criteria: • The death must occur within 30 days of symptom onset in a person with clinical evidence of a measles infection and a positive laboratory test. • The death must not be due to unrelated causes (e.g., motor vehicle accident). • Additional information, such as whether an individual was exposed to a confirmed measles case prior to death or supporting medical records, is also considered. Officials noted a death occurring more than 30 days after the onset of symptoms would not be counted. The department’s update noted the following: • New positive cases since Oct. 14: 38 • Total counties: 43 • Total cumulative cases: 1,260 • Total hospitalizations: 238 • Total confirmed measles-associated deaths: 5 • Measles cases among vaccinated individuals: 4 (less than 1% of cases) According to the department’s dashboard at pa.gov/measles, Lancaster County remains the leader in cases with 452. Cases in the region: Chester County, 91; Lebanon County, 21; Montgomery County, 3; Schuylkill County, 3; and Lehigh County, 2. State health center staff have administered more than 6,100 measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccinations at 210 pop-up vaccination clinics in affected communities since the outbreak began in late April, officials said. Overall, the department has given nearly 9,300 MMR vaccine doses this year. Officials said health care providers continue to see an increase in residents interested in the MMR vaccinations. Providers typically administer about 25,000 doses of the vaccine a month. They said more than 56,000 doses were given in September and that more than 23,000 MMR vaccines were given in the first two weeks of October. The department continues to advise that the best protection against measles is to get fully vaccinated. The two-dose MMR vaccine boosts a person’s immune system and provides 97% lifetime protection, they said. Because measles continues to spread, the department said it recommends an additional early zero dose for infants between the ages of 6 and 11 months who live in or travel to counties flagged on the measles dashboard for sustained community transmission. They said the early dose does not replace the two routine doses. Children 12 months and older who have not received any dose should get one now and a second dose at least 28 days later. Those who have two documented doses of MMR do not need another, the department said. Adults who have only one dose or cannot find their vaccination records should talk with a health care provider or pharmacist about getting vaccinated. Measles is spread when someone who is infected breathes, coughs or sneezes. The virus remains infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after the infected person leaves the area, the department said. Symptoms begin with fever, cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes (conjunctivitis), followed by a rash that starts on the head and spreads downward. Without proper protection or supportive care, measles can be deadly, officials said. Symptoms can start seven to 21 days after exposure. If you believe you were exposed to measles and are experiencing symptoms, you are advised to contact your health care provider or call the health department’s hotline at 877-PA-HEALTH (877-724-3258). Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images Pennsylvania announces sixth death in measles outbreak as case numbers rise Latest fatality is unvaccinated woman, 39, with ‘underlying conditions’ but CDC still lists only two deaths nationwide A sixth death has been announced in Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak, as new figures show cases in the state have risen above 1,100. The most recent fatality was reported in Franklin county on Monday in a statement posted to Facebook by its coroner. The victim was identified as a 39-year-old female who “had several underlying conditions, including a past diagnosis of measles with treatment”. The coroner, James Conner, said it was the first measles-related death in the county “for many years” – and that the patient’s recent diagnosis met the definition of the Pennsylvania health department for inclusion. Five other people have died after contracting measles since August in Pennsylvania, which state officials said on Monday had now recorded 1,137 cases and 219 hospitalizations. The outbreak began west of Philadelphia in April, with authorities blaming low vaccination rates. The federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), however, continues to list deaths nationally at two amid a dispute between the Trump administration’s health secretary, Robert F Kennedy, and Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, over the methodology for classifying measles-related fatalities. Pennsylvania health officials brace for expected spread of measles outbreak Read more The CDC’s website, last updated on Friday, shows 4,080 confirmed measles infections across the US in 42 separate outbreaks, the highest figures in decades, and almost double the number of cases for the whole of 2025. Earlier in October, New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, declared an emergency because of rising case numbers in her state; while Ohio, South Carolina, Texas and Utah have also seen significant increases. A spokesperson for the Pennsylvania health department told NBC News on Monday that it was aware of the Franklin county fatality – and was “conducting a thorough review of the reported death”. The coroner’s office told the outlet through a spokesperson that the woman’s “primary cause of death was a probable acute cardiac event due to possible complications of the measles”. The coroner’s office spokesperson said the woman was not vaccinated. Conner’s statement did not identify the woman to protect the privacy of the victim and relatives. “Families deserve the dignity to mourn in private,” that statement said. “We strongly encourage our medical community, first responders, and the public to follow the precautions set forth by” Pennsylvania state guidelines. Those state guidelines recommend two doses of the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine, or a combined MMRV vaccine including varicella (chickenpox) protection for children 12 and older. The CDC website recommends the same vaccinations, but Kennedy – a longtime vaccine skeptic – has offered mixed messages. In March 2025, he questioned the effectiveness of the measles vaccine, saying people should be able “to make that choice for themselves” about whether to take it. And in September, he told anti-vaccine activists at a conference in Washington DC that they had “a strong and steadfast friend at the White House”, a month after telling US families in response to the rise in measles cases nationwide that parents “should get their children vaccinated”. The Pennsylvania outbreak has seen 157 new cases over the last week, state figures showed, and one-third of the overall number of infections have come in those 18 or under. Fewer than 1% of cases occurred in those who are fully vaccinated. The first two fatalities, reported in August, were infants, one whose mother had measles during her pregnancy, and the second a six-week-old who also had a rare genetic condition. The other Pennsylvania victims were women aged 40 and 20, and an 18-year-old, all of whom had coexisting health conditions. supplementary_news.content: Friday, Oct. 16, 2026 Van Wert weather forecast News Sports Opinion Lifestyles Arts Law Enforcement Real Estate Education Church Obituaries Farm Business-Employment About Us Submit Stories Archives RSS Goal posts have new padding thanks to local bank Pictured from left to right are Eggerss Legacy Chair John White, Suzie Grimes, Terra Bonifas, Ashley Metzger, and Brian Renner from First Federal, and Van Wert Athletic Director Trent Temple.Photo submitted VW independent staff/submitted information While the 2026 high school football regular season winding down, it’s not too late to support the Eggerss Stadium renovation project. That’s just what First Federal of Van Wert is doing. First Fed has purchased the naming rights to the goal post pads in both endzones. “First Federal is proud to be part of the amazing renovation project at Eggerss Stadium,” First Federal President/CEO Brian Renner said. The entire atmosphere is tremendous, and we are excited to be included in the Cougar’s Friday night lights experience.” Now with two locations, First Federal has been serving the community since 1893. “We are fortunate to have partners and supporters like First Federal be part of our transformation,” said John White, Eggerss Legacy Chair. While red and gray are not the organization’s normal color scheme, they agreed to keep the integrity and consistency within the stadium. The next time you attend a game at Eggerss and there’s action near either end zone, First Federal will be front and center for the next score for years to come. “There are still more legacy naming opportunities for businesses or individuals, and we would love to talk to anyone interested,” White said. He can be reached at 419.203.1217 and more information on Legacy naming rights can be found here. (more...) POSTED: 10/15/26 at 8:30 pm Measles case confirmed in Van Wert County Submitted information The Van Wert County General Health District is reporting one laboratory-confirmed case of measles in Van Wert County. The health district is conducting follow-up investigations to identify potential exposures, notify contacts, and provide guidance to individuals who may have been exposed. There are currently 254 confirmed cases of Measles in Ohio as of Tuesday of this week, and 40 cases in Indiana as Wednesday. Measles is a highly contagious viral illness. The measles virus can remain in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. Individuals who are not vaccinated are at highest risk for infection. Symptoms of measles may include a high fever, cough, runny nose, watery or red eyes and a rash. Symptoms generally develop 7–14 days after exposure, however it can take as long as 21 days for symptoms to appear. The onset of symptoms may be delayed in individuals with compromised immune systems. What to do if you have symptoms Avoid contact with others and contact your healthcare provider immediately Call your healthcare provider before arriving at a medical facility and inform them that you may have been exposed to measles or are experiencing symptoms. Calling ahead allows healthcare providers to take appropriate precautions to prevent potential exposure to other patients and staff. Individuals with concerns about symptoms, exposure, or vaccination should contact their healthcare provider or the health district at 419.238.0808 for guidance. How to prevent measles The best way to protect against measles is vaccination. The measles (MMR) vaccination is recommended for anyone age 1 and older who may be unvaccinated to protect themselves and others. Children should get the MMR (Measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine at 12–15 months and again at 4–6 years. Earlier doses (as young as 6 months) may be recommended during special circumstances such as for travel or during outbreaks. Individuals who are unsure of their vaccination status should contact their healthcare provider or the health district to determine whether vaccination is recommended. You are considered protected (immune) if you have one of the following: You were born before 1957, or You have documentation of at least 1 dose of MMR vaccine (two doses are recommended to be considered fully immune), or You have ever had measles diagnosed by a healthcare provider (more...)
