Yes Not now Full Episodes Podcasts Newsletters Live Pennsylvania doctor urges vaccination as measles outbreak grows Oct 15, 2026 6:40 PM EDT By — Jackson Hudgins Jackson Hudgins By — Amna Nawaz Amna Nawaz Leave your feedback Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/pennsylvania-doctor-urges-vaccination-as-measles-outbreak-grows Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Transcript Audio The CDC has confirmed more than 4,000 cases of measles this year as the country grapples with the largest outbreak of the highly infectious virus in 35 years. Nearly a fifth of cases comprise children under the age of five, and 95% are among unvaccinated people. Amna Nawaz spoke with Dr. Evan Shirey, a pediatric infectious disease doctor based in Pennsylvania. Read the Full Transcript Notice: Transcripts are machine and human generated and lightly edited for accuracy. They may contain errors. Amna Nawaz: The CDC has now confirmed more than 4,000 cases of measles this year as the country grapples with the largest outbreak of the highly infectious virus in 35 years. Nearly a fifth of cases comprise children under the age of 5, and more than 90 percent are among people who are unvaccinated. Pennsylvania is the epicenter of the outbreak with more than 1, 100 cases. That includes five measles-related deaths and potentially a sixth still being investigated. For more on what we're seeing and its impact, we're joined now by Dr. Evan Shirey. He's a pediatric infectious disease doctor based in Hershey, Pennsylvania. Dr. Shirey, welcome and thanks for joining us. Dr. Evan Shirey, Penn State Health: Thank you for having me. Amna Nawaz: So you're in Hershey in Central Pennsylvania, the middle of your state's measles epicenter. Just tell us what you're seeing at your hospital right now. Dr. Evan Shirey: Yes, unfortunately, I have been seeing a lot of children and a lot of babies who have been admitted to our hospital and have been very sick. I am seeing the severe consequences that can come from this virus. Amna Nawaz: Tell us about those consequences. What are the measles like in those young children you're seeing? How does it present? Dr. Evan Shirey: So there are a number of complications that can come about from measles. One that we really worry about is encephalitis, and that's when the virus causes infection of the brain. Children with encephalitis from measles in some cases may be unresponsive. In other cases, they may be awake and aware, but confused. They don't know where they are. They're scared, in some cases, not even able to recognize their own parents. These cases are really, really tragic to see. We see infections where the virus infects the lungs or the airways, and we call that a bronchopneumonia. These children might come in breathing really fast, breathing really heavily, gasping for air, in some cases needing different forms of respiratory support and oxygen, and in some of the extreme cases we have seen have even need to be put on a ventilator. We have seen babies who have come in who are unable to nurse or unable to take bottles, and just all forms of various different kinds of suffering from the manifestations of these infections. Amna Nawaz: And, Dr. Shirey, do we know what's driving this outbreak, how it's gotten so severe in Pennsylvania? Dr. Evan Shirey: So we know that, historically, the measles virus caused a lot of infections. We had three or four million infections every single year in this country, and that also resulted in 50,000 hospitalizations, around 500 deaths every year. So we know this is really bad virus. We know the measles virus can spread like wildfire. It is famous for how infectious it is. One person with measles can infect up to 18 others. The reason that we have not been seeing measles cases up until now is because we had a very safe and a very effective vaccine that we had been using for decades that actually resulted in elimination of the virus from this country. The virus is back because of a failure to vaccinate. Amna Nawaz: Given that we thought measles was eliminated about 25 years ago, is this something you ever thought you would be seeing during your time practicing as a doctor? Dr. Evan Shirey: Absolutely not. I spent a lot of time learning about measles as a medical student and as a resident and as an infectious diseases fellow going through all of my training. I always expected that measles was going to stay in the textbooks, and I did not expect that I would live in a world where I was in an ICU taking care of patients in real life. Amna Nawaz: Can I ask you about the rhetoric we're hearing from some of the nation's leaders? I mean, famously, the HHS secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has had some anti-vaccine views and vaccine skepticism he's expressed. How does that complicate your job on the ground? Dr. Evan Shirey: I think it's a real shame. I think that this outbreak just really highlights how important it is that, when we communicate about these important health issues, that we lead with honesty and the truth. I think it's -- overall has been a shame that the anti-vaccine movement has gained the power that they have and that they have gained the influence in reaching ordinary Pennsylvanians. I see in my clinic when I talk to people about vaccines that the types of fears that people have over these last five, 10 years are really just a different dynamic from the way things used to be. And I think that is largely -- unfortunately, it's related to the success of the anti-vaccine movement as a whole. Amna Nawaz: Whenever we cover these kinds of stories, I should mention to you we hear from people who say, look, if you or your children are vaccinated, you will be fine, so there's not much to worry about. What do you make of that argument? Dr. Evan Shirey: So, first and foremost, I want to be very clear that the vaccine is extremely safe and extremely effective. We have been using the MMR vaccine really in the same form since the late 1960s. So we have decades of experience with this. Billions of people have received this vaccine. So I lead with reiterating the truth that the vaccine is very safe and very effective. For people who are vaccinated, I do want to give reassurance, if you are vaccinated, the vaccine is protective. The unfortunate thing that I think people need to understand is that not everyone can receive the vaccine. And so the vulnerable among our communities have been relying for decades on the rest of us to be vaccinated at a high enough rate to achieve herd immunity. One really important point that I can share personally, infants are an important group that can't be vaccinated. And I'm a father of a 2-month-old. He is living in an area where this outbreak is active. And there's nothing that I can do to protect him, rather than -- other than limit his exposures to public places where he may get the virus. Amna Nawaz: Dr. Evan Shirey from Penn State Health joining us tonight. Doctor, thank you so much for your time and your insights. We appreciate it. Dr. Evan Shirey: Of course. Thank you. That person, a “disease detective” within the agency’s Epidemic Intelligence Service, is scheduled to arrive later this week. It’s the CDC’s first in-person assistance to the state after a social media feud in August between Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro. The two traded jabs following a press briefing where Shapiro announced that two unvaccinated people had died of measles complications and accused Kennedy of spreading vaccine misinformation. “I made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric that’s coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America, particularly right here in Pennsylvania,” Shapiro said during the briefing. Kennedy then suggested that the deaths may have been “fabricated,” and that Shapiro was seeking to profit from them politically. Since August, six people diagnosed with measles have died in Pennsylvania, according to health officials and county coroners. The CDC has acknowledged two of the deaths on its measles outbreak website, saying the other measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania are “under review.” “CDC will continue working closely with Pennsylvania health officials to provide the expertise and support needed to respond to the outbreak and protect public health,” a CDC spokesperson wrote in an email Thursday, adding that director Dr. Erica Schwartz recommends the MMR vaccine “as the most effective way to prevent measles and protect against infection.” Pennsylvania is experiencing the nation’s worst measles outbreak in 30 years, with at least 1,222 confirmed cases and 225 hospitalizations, although doctors say the actual number of illnesses is likely much higher. The outbreak’s center remains in Lancaster County, but it is spreading across the state. The Pennsylvania Department of Health did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the CDC aid. The CDC team has previously sent teams to other states with large clusters of measles illnesses: Kansas, New Mexico, South Carolina, Texas, Virginia and Wisconsin. Such deployments are usually short -term, about one to three weeks. supplementary_news.content: Find us on Google 📌 America's birthday 🎂 Start the day smarter ☀️ Get the USA TODAY app U.S. Politics Sports Entertainment Life Money Travel Opinion Crossword ONLY AT USA TODAY: Newsletters For Subscribers Real Estate From the Archives USA TODAY PLAY Crossword Marvel Comics eNewspaper Magazines Investigations Video Podcasts Humankind Advertise Your Business WITNESS (True Crime) Just Curious Best-selling Booklist Top Workplaces Nomination Legals Press Releases Cars Boats Grocery Shopping OUR PORTFOLIO: Real Estate 10BEST USA TODAY Store Shopping Money Essentials Blueprint WITNESS (True Crime) Southern Kitchen Home Internet Services NEWS Ohio Department of Health Add Topic Ohio measles outbreak grows again as Medina County reports 15 cases Chad Murphy James Powel Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY NETWORK Oct. 16, 2026, 10:09 a.m. ET Hear this story Ohio is experiencing its third measles outbreak of 2026, with 252 cases reported across 23 counties so far this year. The number of measles cases in Ohio this year is 460% greater than the total number of cases in 2025. The vast majority of cases in Ohio are among individuals who have not been vaccinated against the disease. Measles has spread to two more Ohio counties as Ohio's third measles outbreak of 2026 continues. The state had 24 new cases in the past week, a 9% increase from the 22 new cases reported the week before, the Ohio Department of Health reports. ODH is reporting 252 cases in 23 counties so far this year, according to its summary of infectious diseases dashboard, updated Oct. 15. That number is 460% greater than the 45 cases reported in all of 2025. Total cases in Ohio this year have continued climbing in recent weeks: 228 cases in 21 counties on Oct. 8 206 cases in 20 counties on Oct. 1 196 cases in 16 counties on Sept. 24 180 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 17 133 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 10 122 cases in 14 counties on Sept. 3 107 cases in 12 counties on Aug. 27 99 cases in 12 counties Aug. 20 69 cases in 11 counties on Aug. 13 45 cases in 10 counties on Aug. 6. Medina (with 15 cases) and Pike (with one case) are the latest counties in Ohio to record new measles cases. Last week, Hancock County joined the list. The week before, Ashland, Stark, Vinton and Wood counties were added. The vast majority of cases in Ohio are among unvaccinated individuals, per ODH. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a July 30 statement. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated.” Measles cases nationwide have hit a 35-year high for a disease once declared eradicated in the United States. Data released Oct. 9 by the Johns Hopkins University shows 4,267 measles cases have been reported nationwide so far this year, surpassing the 2,286 infections recorded during all of 2025 and marking the highest annual total since 1991. Measles growing in Ohio. These counties report cases in 2026 Ohio counties reporting measles cases since Jan. 1, 2026, include: Ashland: 1 Ashtabula: 44 (three new cases) Cuyahoga: 3 Franklin: 8 (one new case) Gallia: 3 Geauga: 52 (two new cases) Hancock: 1 Harrison: 18 (five new cases) Holmes: 9 Knox: 5 Medina: 15 (15 new cases; first time on the list) Meigs: 4 Morgan: 3 Morrow: 13 (one new case) Ottawa: 1 Pike: 1 (one new case; first time on the list) Portage: 1 Stark: 1 Trumbull: 9 (one new case) Tuscarawas: 13 Vinton: 1 Wayne: 45 Wood: 1 The five measles cases listed under "unknown county" last week have been filed to their respective counties in the latest report, bringing the total increase of cases by county to 29. The case count for the year reflects previous outbreaks in Cuyahoga County in January and Franklin County in February. The ages of those with confirmed cases range from 15 months to 20 years old, according to various health departments. Measles cases have been growing in Ohio over the past several years, with one case in 2023, seven in 2024 and 45 cases in 2025. Pennsylvania reports measles deaths At least five people this year have died from measles in Pennsylvania as of Sept. 30, 2026, according to USA TODAY. None of the individuals were vaccinated, USA TODAY reports. The first two measles deaths were the first in Pennsylvania in 35 years, the state Department of Health said in an Aug. 25 news release, and the first such deaths in the United States this year, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. Where are measles cases spreading in Ohio? Hancock County Public Health reported one measles case in Findlay with possible exposure to the public at NWO Urgent Care on September 29 from 2:30–5:30 p.m. and Blanchard Valley Hospital Emergency Department the same day from 3:30–6:30 p.m. Geauga Public Health reports that individuals with measles visited several locations while able to spread the virus, including Bloomfield Horse Sale, 2211 Kinsman Road NW, on July 18. The Tuscarawas health department reports that another of its cases was exposed at the Bloomfield Livestock Auction, at the same address as Bloomfield Horse Sale, on on the same day. Measles cases hit 35-year high in United States The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to USA TODAY, citing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. Health experts say the recent surge has been fueled by declining vaccination rates that have left more communities vulnerable to outbreaks. Measles cases on the rise as Ohio vaccination rates fluctuate in state, U.S. Vaccination rates for measles have declined in recent years, resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated. Most people are then protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners decreased from 95.2% during the 2019–20 school year to 92.5% in the 2024–25 school year, well under the threshold necessary for effective herd immunity, according to the CDC. Ohio's vaccination rate for the 2025-26 school year slipped well below the herd immunity threshold, making it susceptible to outbreaks. In Ohio, MMR vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — coverage rate for children and adolescents was 91.5% for 2023. Previous years ranged from an 80% to 90% immunization rate: 2019: 81.8% 2020: 88.0% 2021: 91.7% 2022: 89.0% Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventive measures, such as the use of vitamin A. During the height of the Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. Kennedy is now encouraging the measles vaccine. Trump signs executive order to separate MMR vaccine President Donald Trump in August 2026 signed an executive order to split the childhood measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three shots and delivering them at separate medical visits as well as "calling for more vaccine flexibility and research" and fewer childhood vaccinations, according to USA TODAY. "You have the MMR, we want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together there could be a possibility they're quite lethal and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal, but just very effective," said Trump from the Oval Office as he signed the order. But the MMR vaccine is not lethal, and medical research shows no health benefit or reduced risk from splitting it. In contrast, separating the shots increases injection pain, leaves children unprotected longer, and lowers overall vaccination rates, according to experts. The MMR vaccine has been in existence since 1971, according to the World Health Organization. Can you get measles if vaccinated? Two doses of MMR are 97% effective against measles, ODH reports. If you are up to date on the measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low. Are measles deadly? Measles can be deadly. ODH states that complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. What does measles look like? Signs, symptoms Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, but it can take up to 21 days. Symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, a swelling of the brain, may also occur. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. If other people breathe the contaminated air or touch an infected surface and then touch their eyes, noses, or mouths, they can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before, through four days after, a rash appears. Are measles itchy? Not usually, according to the Cleveland Clinic. How to protect yourself against measles Both ODH and the CDC say the best way to protect yourself against measles is to be vaccinated. USA TODAY reporters James Powel and Mary Walrath-Holdridge contributed to this report. Featured Weekly Ad

(WAFF) - A confirmed measles case in Huntsville has raised questions about possible exposure at two businesses along Bailey Cove Road, but doctors say vaccination offers strong protection and there is reason to hope the exposure remains limited. A person infected with measles visited a Subway and Publix earlier this month, according to the Alabama Department of Public Health. Dr. William Schaffner, an infectious disease expert at Vanderbilt Health, explained that while those visits happened earlier this month, people who were exposed and are not protected against measles could still develop symptoms. “It’s possible that there could be some persons who were susceptible who might still come down with measles,” Schaffner said. “We’re getting out to the end of the what we call the incubation period, and so every day that goes by, the risk goes down.” Schaffner explained that measles spreads through the air, not by touching products or other surfaces inside a business. “The measles virus is so contagious it can hover in the air for up to two hours,” Schaffner said. That means someone susceptible to measles could have been exposed even after the infected person left. “So somebody could come into that room and inhale that air even an hour, hour and a half later,” Schaffner said. “And if they’re susceptible, they could become infected with the virus.” Schaffner also addressed concerns from vaccinated parents with children who may be too young to receive their first measles vaccine. He explained that people who are immune through vaccination or a previous infection do not simply carry the virus home and transmit it to their children. For those who are susceptible, symptoms may take a week or longer to appear. Schaffner expects health officials to remain particularly alert for additional cases over the next three to four weeks. Meanwhile, Huntsville Hospital had already discussed how it would care for measles patients before the local case was confirmed. Dr. Jessica Branscome, medical director of the hospital’s pediatric emergency department, said staff held meetings as measles cases increased elsewhere in the country to prepare for the possibility of patients needing treatment locally. Since the confirmed case, the hospital has received questions from people concerned about possible exposure. Those inquiries are being referred to the Alabama Department of Public Health, which coordinates measles testing. Despite the possibility of additional cases, Branscome believes the exposure may remain limited. “I wouldn’t be concerned yet,” Branscome said. “I think we only have one case, and I think it will end up hopefully just being a limited exposure, so I wouldn’t be worried yet.” Branscome pointed to Alabama’s vaccination rate as one reason for her optimism. She estimated that about 95% of kindergarteners entering public schools across the state are vaccinated against measles, helping provide broader protection throughout the community. For people concerned about possible exposure, Branscome recommends watching for symptoms that may initially resemble the flu, including a runny nose, before a rash develops. Anyone who believes they were exposed and begins experiencing symptoms should call a healthcare provider before arriving for an evaluation, Branscome advised. Calling ahead allows medical staff to take precautions to avoid exposing other patients. Huntsville Hospital is not offering routine measles testing through its emergency rooms, which Branscome emphasized should remain available for medical emergencies. The Alabama Department of Public Health reviews possible exposures and determines when measles testing is appropriate. Read Full Bio Conor Wight Updated on: October 15, 2026 / 10:50 PM CDT / CBS Minnesota Add CBS News on Google The Minnesota Department of Health says it has identified two separate measles outbreaks in southeastern and central Minnesota, leaded to 25 cases in the last month. The clusters in Fillmore and Todd counties in recent weeks make up more than half of the measles cases in Minnesota this year. According to the state's department of health, all the people who got sick were unvaccinated. Beth Parilla, who manages the Vaccine Preventable Diseases Section with the Minnesota Department of Health, said that the clusters in Fillmore and Todd counties are unrelated to one another but began in similar ways. She said that in each county, they began with someone picking up measles while travelling elsewhere in the United States and bringing the disease back to communities with low vaccination rates. "The more people that get measles, the more likely we are to see people with severe complications," Parilla said, "with a disease like this, we will do our best, but it is really hard to contain measles." Jackie Och, the Health and Human Services Director in Todd County, said that her team is concerned about declining MMR vaccine rates in children. As of 2021, the county reported a vaccine rate amongst children born that year of 74.6%; that rate dropped to 61.6% by 2023. Parilla said that given how contagious measles are, vaccination rates need to be near 100 percent to prevent spread. "It spreads really really fast. and we have a lot of groups in Minnesota that now have concerningly low immunization coverage," Parilla said. Linda Widmer said that she wishes she had the vaccine available to her when she was a young child. Widmer said that she was vacationing at a Minnesota lake at the age of seven when she found herself fighting an incredibly high fever for up to five days thanks to a measles infection. She believes the prolonged fever impacted her brain long-term. "I felt terrible and just stayed in bed," Widmer said, "I was miserable and I couldn't go out and play. It was terrible." This was 1955; the vaccine became available to the public in 1963. By the year 2000, the United States declared the disease eradicated within the country. Among the more than 4,000 cases recorded in 2026 in the United States, Wisconsin's Department of Health Services has confirmed at least 267 cases. Measles, which was eliminated in the U.S. for decades, is classified by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as one of the most contagious infectious diseases. The best way to prevent the disease is through vaccination, the department of health says. "There are pockets of unvaccinated or under-vaccinated people across Minnesota, and anyone who isn't vaccinated against measles is at risk, especially right now," the health department said in a statement. Overall, the U.S. has seen 4,000 cases of measles this year. Forty-two of those cases have happened in Minnesota. Last year, Minnesota saw 26 total cases. In a statement, the county coroner’s office office said the woman had underlying medical conditions, though it did not provide specifics. A spokesperson for the Franklin County coroner’s office said the “primary cause of death was a probable acute cardiac event due to possible complications of the measles.” Cardiac complications from measles can happen, but they are uncommon. The woman had not been vaccinated, the spokesperson said. The state’s Health Department considers a death to be “measles-associated” if it occurred within 30 days of symptom onset and there is clinical evidence of a measles infection and a positive laboratory test. It also takes into account the person’s medical records and whether they were exposed to measles before they died. The measles virus under a microscope. BSIP / Universal Images Group via Getty As of Friday, Pennsylvania had confirmed 1,136 measles cases , with 219 hospitalizations. Two-thirds of those cases were diagnosed in adults. The Health Department said in an email Monday that it was aware of the Franklin County coroner’s announcement and “is conducting a thorough review of the reported death.” The death announced Monday is the sixth in less than two months in the state, suggesting the outbreak is far greater than reported. Historically, measles infections cause 1 to 2 deaths per 1,000 cases. “I think we’re probably closer to 6,000 cases,” said Dr. Paul Offit, a pediatrician and director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “They are vastly underestimating the number of cases. It’s much worse.” The first two deaths announced in the state in late August were in infants, both in Lancaster County, which has accounted for the vast majority of cases in the state’s outbreak. One father in Lancaster County told NBC News that his wife was sick with measles in August and went into labor a month early. Their baby died shortly after birth. The other was a 6-week-old who had a rare genetic condition. Last month, a 40-year-old woman with asthma and severe lung disease died in Jefferson County, as well as an 18-year-old Mifflin County resident who died “due to complications of measles,” specifically a rare and severe neurological condition that causes inflammation in the brain. The Philadelphia Inquirer reported in early October that the fifth death occurred in a 20-year-old woman with a compromised immune system because of leukemia. The vast majority of people diagnosed with measles are unvaccinated. According to the Pennsylvania Department of Health, less than 1% of cases there occurred in people who were fully vaccinated. The first dose of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is typically given at around 1 year of age and then around age 5. Two doses offer 97% protection against measles, usually for life. During outbreaks, babies as young as 6 months old are eligible for a dose ahead of those two recommended shots. Nationally, there have been 4,080 measles cases this year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. It’s the most cases since 1991

Advertisement Updated: 5:20 AM EDT Oct 14, 2026 Editorial Standards i Alex Suckow Digital Media Manager Measles cases surge past 150 in Kentucky; big outbreak identified in one county Updated: 5:20 AM EDT Oct 14, 2026 Editorial Standards i Alex Suckow Digital Media Manager LAUREL COUNTY, Ky. — Just days after Kentucky's measles case count hit 100, dozens more have been reported. As of Wednesday, the number of cases reported in the Commonwealth is now 157 for 2026. Advertisement Most of those come out of Laurel County, which had seven cases just a few days ago. Now, it has 56, according to the state's dashboard . Laurel County is in southeast Kentucky. The dashboard says that outbreak involves people who are unvaccinated from several large households that have been "isolated from the broader community." This content is imported from infogram. You may be able to find the same content in another format, or you may be able to find more information, at their web site. In only one case did the person report having the full vaccine. One case had one MMR dose, and the rest didn't have any. Of the total state count, nine of those cases have led to hospitalization. So far, no deaths have been reported. There were only 13 cases overall in 2025, and none were reported the year prior. What to know about measles Measles is a disease caused by a highly contagious virus. It is spread through the air when someone with measles sneezes, coughs, or breathes. Symptoms include high fever, cough, runny nose, red and watery eyes, and rash. Tiny white spots can appear inside the mouth two to three days after symptoms begin. The disease can be especially severe in infants, pregnant women, and people who have weakened immune systems. While rare, measles can result in death. What Kentucky health officials are saying Kentucky health officials have warned this is the highest case count in decades. Dr. Steve Stack, with the Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services, along with other local health officials, has been encouraging people to get vaccinated. "We do not need to have measles," Gov. Andy Beshear said last month. "We have a proven tool that for over a quarter century eliminated it from the United States. The only reason it's resurging now is because of, I think, negligent information and guidance being shared freely. We want people to not feel vilified or maligned. We want people to feel informed." supplementary_news.content: Skip to main content News 3 measles cases reported in Wright County as the illness increases nationwide KSMU | By Michele Skalicky, Chris Drew Published October 14, 2026 at 4:45 PM CDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email A map of measles cases in the U.S. as of October 8, 2026. Kindergarten vaccination rates have been dropping as measles cases jump. Measles cases are up nationwide – and in Missouri. On Wednesday, the Wright County Health Department shared on social media that it had confirmed three measles cases. In its statement, the health department said the cases “were evaluated by local healthcare providers and tested positive for measles. Persons with known possible exposures are being contacted. Details of potential public exposures have been limited thus far. Additional information will be provided as it becomes available.” Wright County said it is working in collaboration with the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services. As of Wednesday, the CDC had reported 4,080 measles cases nationwide this year, a significant uptick from last year’s total of 2,289. Kendra Findley, BCBH program coordinator for the Taney County Health Department, said measles is highly contagious and potentially dangerous. According to Findley, a person with measles can potentially spread the illness to 18 vulnerable and unvaccinated people. "So, I mean, if you can picture what that looks like for every one case, you could have 18 cases, how quickly that could explode within a population as far as the amount of disease," she said. "And measles isn't just an inconvenient rash illness, you know, in children, up to 30% of cases will have serious complications with the disease. So it is something to think about. It is something to prepare for." Stephanie Woehl, administrator of communicable disease prevention at the Springfield-Greene County Health Department, said there’s an easy way to prevent the illness. "We have a really great tool to help protect ourselves and our community from measles in the MMR vaccine," she said. "So the vaccine that's measles, mumps and rubella, that vaccine has a really high efficacy. It works really well to help protect us from the measles virus...it's very effective, and it's very safe. It is one of it is our best tools in our toolbox to help keep ourselves and our community safe from this virus." She encourages anyone who has questions about the vaccine to talk with their health care provider. Findley said the Taney County Health Department is working to spread the word about the safety and effectiveness of the vaccine as measles cases continue to rise. "For a long time, it was a disease that we didn't really have to think about too much because there wasn't much of it...circulating within the community," she said. "But as vaccination rates have dropped, you're starting to see it pop up and start circulating as they're seeing this year with that measles outbreak across the United States. So, you know, the best method of prevention is the vaccine, which has been proven safe and effective." Woehl said there’s been a steady decline in vaccination rates over the last few years. Missouri’s kindergarten vaccination rate for 2025 was 89.5%, down from nearly 95% in 2019. The Wright County kindergarten vaccination rate was reported at 81.4% last year. According to the CDC and the World Health Organization, a community needs a vaccination rate of at least 95% to be adequately protected from measles outbreaks. "I think it's multifaceted," Woehl said about why vaccine rates have dropped. "There are a lot of reasons, and it's usually very individualized, but there is a lot of information about vaccines in various media forms. There are challenges with access. Questions arise around safety and efficacy. So there's not a, I think, one size fits all to why we're seeing that decline." Three measles cases were reported in Greene County earlier this year. Taney County hasn’t yet seen a measles case this year. The state currently reports a total of 14 measles cases in Missouri in 2026. Missouri reported 6 total cases in 2025 and 2 in 2024. Signs and symptoms According to the CDC, measles symptoms appear 7 to 14 days after contact with the virus. Measles typically begins with: High fever (may spike to more than 104 degrees) cough runny nose red, watery eyes 2–3 days after symptoms begin: Koplik spots Tiny white spots (Koplik spots) may appear inside the mouth two to three days after symptoms begin. 3–5 days after symptoms begin: measles rash Measles rash appears 3 to 5 days after the first symptoms. It usually begins as flat red spots that appear on the face at the hairline. They then spread downward to the neck, trunk, arms, legs, and feet. Small, raised bumps may also appear on top of the flat, red spots. The spots may become joined together as they spread from the head to the rest of the body. When the rash appears, a person's fever may spike to more than 100 degrees. Contact your healthcare provider if you suspect measles. Pittsburgh-area medical experts explain the symptoms. By John Shumway John Shumway Anchor/Reporter John Shumway joined KDKA in October 1988 as a General Assignment Reporter. During his years at KDKA, he has anchored the morning and weekend news and is currently a featured General Assignment Reporter on the station's 4, 5 and 6 p.m. newscasts. Read Full Bio John Shumway Updated on: October 14, 2026 / 12:32 PM EDT / CBS Pittsburgh Add CBS News on Google Many health experts find themselves increasingly concerned about the outbreak of measles in Pennsylvania. Now, with a confirmed case in Allegheny County, there is little doubt that other cases are out there and that it is extremely contagious. When someone is infected with measles, they can be contagious and not even know the risk. As an airborne virus, measles flies on the fall breeze, and we have no way of knowing it's there. "It's the most contagious virus that we know; we have no other viral infection like this," said Dr. Robert Jacobson of the Mayo Clinic. "One of the other tricks of this virus, this respiratory particle, is that it can hang in the air for two hours after the infected person leaves the room," Dr. Robert Jacobson said. "This means an unrecognized case of measles - a person who just has runny, watery eyes, nose, and a cough with a fever those first few days - they're spreading the respiratory droplets in every room and hallway they're in and leaving it hanging in the air." "It's in the air, you breathe it in, and there you go," added Dr. Jillian Irwin, the Allegheny County Health Department's medical director. When is measles contagious? Dr. Irwin said it can be anywhere between 7 and 21 days from exposure before you start showing symptoms. "Four days before they get the telltale rash, and four days after," Dr. Irwin said of the contagious period. "The day you get the rash is [day] zero." According to Dr. Irwin, if you've received the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine or had measles as a child, you should be OK. She said that 9 out of 10 people who have not been vaccinated will contract measles. According to the CDC, one out of five of those people will end up in the hospital. If you know that you have been exposed to measles but haven't been vaccinated, you can get the vaccine within three days. Measles infection can be serious "There's no guarantee that you're going to know if you are exposed within three days," Dr. Irwin explained. "That is why it's not worth the risk. People can get pneumonia; they can get brain swelling; it's a pretty severe situation. While it's not common, it's why we worry about measles." When it comes to the case of the child being exposed to measles at Target in McCandless, Dr. Irwin said they knew they were cutting it close with the warning. "There was one more day before people could potentially get immunoglobulin to help prevent measles," she said. That window is now closed. Dr. Irwin said this is very serious as now five people in Pennsylvania have died during this outbreak of measles. She said don't just assume it's a cold if you get a cough, runny nose, and watery eyes -- they could be symptoms leading up to the measles rash. All the latest info Keith Demko Salisbury Daily Times Oct. 13, 2026, 8:38 a.m. ET Measles cases in Maryland have grown almost 20-fold in 2026 over the total for 2025, with 56 measles cases in the state as of Oct. 8. Here's everthing to know about the current state of Measles in Maryland, from the Maryland Department of Health's Center for Immunization. What is Measles? Measles is a highly contagious, vaccine-preventable viral illness that causes a high fever with a full-body rash. Measles infection can affect the body's respiratory immune, and central nervous systems. The best way to protect yourself, your family and your community from measles is to get vaccinated. How many Measles cases in Maryland for 2026 vs. previous years? The MD Department of Health has reported 56 cases of Maryland in 2026 so far, after just three in all of 2025. Here are the state's totals back to 2017 2024: 1 2023: 1 2022: 0 2021: 0 2020: 0 2019: 5 2018: 1 2017: 1 What are the symptoms of Measles? Early symptoms of measles are high fever; runny nose; cough; and red, watery eyes. Usually, one to four days after the early symptoms, a red rash appears on the face and spreads to the rest of the body. Some people may suffer from severe complications, such as pneumonia (infection of the lungs) and encephalitis (swelling of the brain). They may need to be hospitalized and could die. Measles may cause pregnant women to give birth prematurely, or have a low-birth-weight baby. How is Measles transmitted from person to person? Measles spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes, and the measles virus can live for up to two hours in an airspace where the infected person has coughed or sneezed. A person with measles is contagious beginning four days before the rash appears until four days after the rash begins. Measles symptoms typically develop 10-14 days after exposure to the virus. High vaccination rates in schools are crucial for preventing outbreaks and maintaining community immunity. Maryland maintains a strong safety net with 96.7% of kindergarteners reported as vaccinated in the 2025-2026 school year. What to know about Measles vaccine in Maryland The MMR vaccine is safe and effective, providing about 97% protection after two doses. Some formulations of the vaccine (MMRV) include protection against varicella, or chicken pox, as well. Vaccination of Children: Measles can be prevented with the MMR (Measles, Mumps, Rubella) vaccine. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that children receive their first dose between 12 and 15 months of age, followed by a second dose at 4 to 6 years old. However, if you or your child missed a dose, you can still complete the series at any time. If you are planning international travel with a child under six months, children aged 6 through 11 months should receive one dose of the MMR vaccine before international travel or travel to areas with an ongoing outbreak to ensure early protection. Caregivers should consult their healthcare provider to determine if the child is eligible for this early dose. Note: This early dose does not count toward the routine series, so the child will still require their standard doses at 12 to 15 months and 4 to 6 years. For more information about Maryland’s childhood vaccination recommendations, including measles, see the Maryland Childhood Immunization Schedule. For more information about the measles vaccine for children, see the American Academy of Pediatrics Measles: What Parents Need to Know. For more information on the safety of the measles vaccine, see the American Academy of Pediatrics MMR Fact Checked page. For more information about prevention during outbreaks or international travel, see the American Academy of Pediatrics Measles Prevention and Control Implementation. Vaccination of Adults: Adults born before 1957 are generally considered immune to measles. Those born in 1957 or later should have documentation of at least one MMR dose or other evidence of immunity, such as a "titer" blood test. However, some adults, including healthcare workers, international travelers, college students, and close contacts of immunocompromised people, require two doses separated by at least 28 days. Adults who are unsure of their vaccination history should talk to their doctor. For more information about Maryland’s adult vaccination recommendations, including measles, see the Maryland Adult Immunization Schedule. She is an Emmy-winning journalist and visual storyteller with a passion for telling stories that matter. Read Full Bio Grace Manthey Updated on: October 12, 2026 / 11:58 AM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google So far in 2026, the U.S. has recorded the most measles cases in more than three decades as outbreaks spread in multiple states, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. By mid-July, the number had already surpassed all of 2025, which had been the worst year in recent history with more than 2,200 confirmed cases. By early October, the number of cases topped 4,000. Ongoing outbreaks have put the U.S. at risk of losing its official measles elimination status, which it has held since 2000. In August, health officials in Pennsylvania reported the state's first two deaths connected to measles in 35 years, both in Lancaster County. Both of the individuals were not vaccinated against the virus, state health officials said. Several more deaths associated with measles were later reported as the state's outbreak surged to over 1,000 confirmed cases. Measles is one of the most contagious infectious diseases. In some cases, it can cause severe infections in the lungs and brain that can lead to cognitive issues, deafness or death. But it can be prevented by vaccination, which medical research has proven to be safe and highly effective. The CBS News data team has tracked confirmed measles cases nationwide as new data is released by state health departments and the CDC. Out of the 2,289 confirmed cases last year, more than 750 were connected to an outbreak in West Texas that led to the deaths of two children. Prior to 2025, the highest number of confirmed cases in the U.S. in recent years was 1,274 in 2019, driven by outbreaks in New York, California and Washington state. Most years, the total was much lower. Health experts point to lower vaccination rates as the main reason for increases in preventable infectious diseases like measles. The vast majority of cases have been in people who were unvaccinated, and outbreaks have spread in communities with lower vaccination rates. CDC data shows about 92.4% of kindergartners in the U.S. got their measles-mumps-rubella shots in the 2025-2026 school year, down slightly from 92.5% the previous year. The figure has declined from 95.2% during the 2019-2020 school year — a critical threshold to keep people safe. Only 10 states hit the 95% threshold last year. "When more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated, most people are protected through community immunity (herd immunity)," the CDC states. "I think that parents, for most kids, especially for the measles vaccines, the DTP, all the standard childhood vaccines, it's very important that parents vaccinate their kids," Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, the director of the National Institutes of Health, said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan." Research has found no evidence of increased rates of autism among those who are vaccinated compared to those who are not. Vaccines also undergo intensive safety testing. A 39-year-old woman from Chambersburg, Pa., who had been diagnosed with measles has died. The woman is the sixth person to die with measles amid a historic statewide outbreak in Pennsylvania. The Franklin County Coroner confirmed the news in a press release Monday. “This is the first death in Franklin County in many years with a patient with a recent history of measles diagnosis,” Franklin County Coroner Jordan Conner, a Republican, said in a statement. The office said it investigated the death Saturday and found that the woman had several underlying conditions including a previous case of measles that had been treated. The office declined to specify what other underlying conditions were apparent from the investigation. Officials declined to identify the woman or disclose whether anyone may have been exposed to the virus as a result of interacting with her. It’s unclear whether the woman had been vaccinated against measles. Pennsylvania’s statewide measles outbreak climbed to more than 1,130 cases as of late last week. According to the state health department, 219 people have been hospitalized. Conner urged the public to adhere to medical guidance from the Pennsylvania Department of Health, which has been hosting dozens of popup vaccination clinics to boost immunity. “Caution and vigilance are key to our success in the treatment of this disease and its after [effects],” Conner said. Wake Up With The Facts Inbox Edition: A 5-minute morning read, covering the Pittsburgh news that impacts your life. Measles has not been as widespread in Franklin County as compared to other counties in Central and Southeastern Pennsylvania. As of late last week, the county has only recorded seven cases of measles. The Chambersburg woman is the sixth death recorded as part of the outbreak. But state and federal officials have clashed over how to characterize the climbing number of measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania. A measles-associated death is defined by state officials as one that occurs within 30 days of symptom onset and with clinical evidence of an infection such as a positive laboratory test. The death can not be due to other unrelated causes such as a car accident. But the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has only recognized two measles-associated deaths nationwide. The agency’s website does not say where the deaths occurred, but Pennsylvania is the only state to have reported fatal measles cases so far this year. supplementary_news.content: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Thursday defended the Trump administration’s response to recent measles deaths in Pennsylvania, saying the United States has done better than other countries fighting what he said is a global measles outbreak. “It’s all over the world,” Kennedy said in answer to a reporter’s question about his agency’s response to the Pennsylvania outbreak at an unrelated event in Virginia. Kennedy said the United States has had 4,000 measles cases this year compared with 20,000 cases in Mexico and 7,000 in Canada. According to the World Health Organization, Bangladesh leads the world with 65,439 cases reported in the last six months; Mexico ranked 7th, with 6,844 cases. The Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy said last week that the U.S. is on track to double last year’s measles cases because of declining vaccination rates, as the U.S. endures its worst year for the disease since 1991. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, there have been 4,080 confirmed measles cases in the U.S. in 2026 resulting from 42 measles outbreaks, the largest being in Pennsylvania. The United States has seen eight reported measles-associated deaths in the last two years ‚ more than the combined total of reported deaths over the previous three decades. Of those, five have been in Pennsylvania, according to the state’s Health Department. A sixth measles-associated death was reported over the weekend that the state is currently reviewing. “I am confident I will bring that outbreak to a quick close,” Kennedy said. Pennsylvania has reported 1,222 measles illnesses so far this year across 42 counties, the state Health Department reported Wednesday. None of the people who died were vaccinated, according to the department. The nation eliminated the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. “The measles outbreak is occurring because so many people went unvaccinated during the COVID pandemic,” Kennedy said, attributing the idea to Dr. Anthony Fauci, who served on the White House Coronavirus Task Force starting in early 2020. In the roughly 1,000 pages of Fauci’s COVID-era journal released in July, through of a subpoena filed by Republican Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul, Fauci said he worried children would miss their measles vaccinations because of COVID shutdowns. On Thursday, Kennedy blamed Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro for failing to accept assistance from the CDC’s emergency Epi-Aid program — assistance Shapiro requested in September but made conditional on the CDC recognizing that four measles-associated deaths the state had reported be included in the federal agency’s Measles Cases and Outbreaks dashboard. Kennedy said that issue was resolved this week. On Tuesday, the CDC announced it would deploy a “disease detective” to help bring the outbreak to an end. The Associated Press contributed to this report

By Kayla See Published: Oct. 15, 2026 at 12:04 AM UTC Share Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google MADISON, Wis. (WMTV) - As measles cases continue to rise across Wisconsin, hospitals in Madison are preparing for what happens when someone with the highly contagious virus comes in for care. As of Oct. 13, the Wisconsin Department of Health Services had reported 267 confirmed measles cases statewide this year. Measles can remain in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves a room. That creates a particular challenge for hospitals and clinics, where patients may already be sick or have weakened immune systems. At UnityPoint Health–Meriter, Infection Prevention Manager Katelyn Harms said staff are trained to identify possible measles cases quickly. Patients are screened for symptoms including fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes and a rash that typically starts on the face and spreads down the body. Staff also check vaccination histories. If someone is suspected of having measles, the goal is to separate them from other patients as quickly as possible. “In the case that we find someone who would be suspected for disease, our team members are going to quickly put them in designated airborne isolation rooms or negative pressure rooms,” Harms said. “Those are rooms especially designed to contain the air in that space.” These rooms use specialized ventilation to help prevent contaminated air from spreading into other parts of the hospital. Staff caring for patients with suspected measles also wear protective respirators. But not every medical facility has a negative-pressure room. Harms said smaller clinics have other options, including keeping patients in separate rooms, using portable HEPA air filters and scheduling appointments at the end of the day after other patients have left. At UW Health, preparation began before Wisconsin’s current rise in measles cases. Dr. Dan Shirley, an infectious disease physician at UW Health, said staff started practicing how they would respond to a possible measles patient as cases appeared elsewhere and vaccination rates declined. “We started doing some preparations. So we would do kind of practice runs of what we would do if measles came into the clinic or the hospital,” Shirley said. Those exercises include planning how to move a contagious patient through the hospital without exposing visitors, staff or other patients. Shirley said preventing exposure is especially important in a hospital setting. “It’s even more complicated in a hospital where we have a concentration of vulnerable patients who are already sick and maybe immunocompromised,” he said. Some patients, including infants too young to be vaccinated and people with weakened immune systems, face a greater risk of serious complications from measles. Shirley emphasized that the danger extends beyond the person who initially becomes infected. “It’s one thing for you if you’re a normal healthy person to get measles, but you then can spread it to other people who are vulnerable and may have a bad outcome from it,” he said. What to do if you think you have measles Both hospitals emphasize the importance of calling ahead before visiting a clinic or emergency department if you suspect you have measles. That gives medical staff time to prepare for your arrival, arrange a safer way to evaluate you and reduce the chance of exposing others. Health officials also continue to recommend vaccination as the best protection against measles. According to the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine are about 97% effective at preventing measles. More information about measles symptoms, vaccination and Wisconsin’s latest case numbers is available on the Wisconsin DHS website⁠. The child’s cheek shows the characteristic rash associated with this viral infection. Cayuga, Cortland, Madison, Oswego, Ontario, Seneca, Wayne, Yates, Rockland, Nassau, Herkimer, Montgomery, Ostego, Essex, Lewis, Chemung, Chenango, Steuben, Tioga, Allegany, Chautauqua, and Erie. If you’re thinking: that’s a long list of counties in New York, you’re right. That’s 22 of New York’s 62 counties. And this year alone, they’ve all had measles cases. This week on the Disabilities Beat, we speak with experts on what measles is, why cases are rising in New York, the risks, and what the state is doing. TRANSCRIPT This is a rush transcript produced by a contractor and may be updated over time to be more accurate. Emyle Watkins: Hi, I'm Emyle Watkins, and this is the Disabilities Beat. There are 62 counties in New York State. 22 of them have had recorded measles cases this year alone. Erie and Chautauqua counties are among them. Dr. John Sellick: I get the text message that we think we might have another measles, then I'm concerned that did this get missed along the way and are we going to start seeing secondary cases? Emyle Watkins: That's Dr. John Sellick, Kaleida Health's hospital epidemiologist. He says most people have never seen measles firsthand. The last cases he saw personally were when he and his brother caught it as children in the 1960s. Dr. John Sellick: There were none of the vaccines available when I was a kid. I still remember having measles and I still remember having mumps. Emyle Watkins: There have been over a hundred cases of measles in New York so far this year. That may seem like a small number, but measles is 12 times more contagious than the flu, making the risk high enough that Governor Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency last week. Dr. John Sellick: Measles is highly contagious. It's one of the most contagious infectious diseases that we have in humans. Emyle Watkins: Sellick and two other infectious disease experts BTPM interviewed say most people don't know measles doesn't start with the notorious rash. Dr. John Sellick: They get in through our respiratory tract, but the reason you have rash is because the virus is spreading throughout your body. Emyle Watkins: At Erie County Medical Center, senior vice president of nursing, Charlene Ludlow, has more than 30 years of experience in infection control. She says measles starts like many other respiratory illnesses. Charlene Ludlow: They got a high fever, they've got respiratory symptoms, but then three or four days later, here comes the rash that says, "Uh-oh, this isn't the flu. This isn't something else. This is measles." By that point, now you've got people exposed. Emyle Watkins: Symptoms typically start one to two weeks after you're exposed to measles, beginning with a high fever, cough, runny nose, and red watery eyes. Some people will have white spots in their mouth two to three days later. The rash comes three to five days after the initial symptoms, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Charlene Ludlow: I still think the most important part of the fall is those people with fevers staying home. Emyle Watkins: There is no treatment for measles. One in five unvaccinated people who get measles are hospitalized, and one in 20 children with measles develop pneumonia. Measles can also cause encephalitis or brain swelling, lifelong disabilities or death. Charlene Ludlow: It can be death, it can be encephalitis, it can be things that will change life forever for people. And the level of contagiousness of this disease is so high. Emyle Watkins: The reason we haven't seen measles in so long is because of the highly effective and safe vaccine. Charlene Ludlow: The state of Pennsylvania, they've had about 975 cases already, and they've had five children die. I mean, that's a huge number in my mind. I mean, any child obviously, but this is vaccine preventable. And the majority of the cases they're seeing of this disease is happening in the unvaccinated population. Emyle Watkins: Only three in every 100 people who get the vaccine experience a breakthrough case of measles after exposure, and that's usually in people who are immunocompromised or who have prolonged exposure to someone with measles. And even in these cases, vaccination makes the illness more mild. Dr. John Sellick: With the current MMR vaccine, we have now pretty close to a half a century, 50 years worth, actually more than that for some of them, of good solid data that shows that these are safe. There have been literally dozens of studies and re-analysis of studies showing that there's no link between vaccination and autism, especially measles vaccine and autism. Emyle Watkins: Local state of emergency allows paramedics, pharmacists, midwives, and other medical professionals to administer the vaccine, and nurses can now order measles tests. Experts we spoke to say these changes could help reach rural and insular communities with low vaccination. Dr. John Sellick: Many of the outbreaks that we see, for instance, are in rural remote populations, especially Amish where there's aversion to traditional medicine. Emyle Watkins: Dr. Sellick says the risks are higher now than the last time measles was prevalent. Modern medicine allows people to live longer and healthier, but we also have a larger high risk population. Dr. John Sellick: So now you have these very large populations of people who are very susceptible because of cancer, treatment of cancer, treatment of other diseases. So this is why it's so important to maintain those very high levels of immunity. Emyle Watkins: Next week on the Disabilities Beat, we will tackle understanding your risk and what to do if you're feeling anxious about measles or are unsure of the vaccine. I'm Emyle Watkins. Thanks for listening. supplementary_news.content_title: Wright County Announces Three Measles Cases Reported
supplementary_news.content: Hartville, MO. – The Wright County Health Department announced this morning that three cases of measles have been reported, and have addressed it in an official press release. The release can be read below. ————————————————————————————————- Three cases of measles have been reported to the Wright County Health Department. These ill persons were evaluated by local healthcare providers and tested positive for measles. Persons with known possible exposures are being contacted. Details of potential public exposures have been limited thus far. Additional information will be provided as it becomes available. The Wright County Health Department is working in collaboration with the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services. All individuals with possible exposures should watch for the symptoms of measles for 21 days from the date of exposure and contact their local public health agency if symptoms appear. People who think they have measles should isolate themselves and call their health care provider before arriving to be evaluated and to receive care. It is important to let the healthcare facility and medical providers know of the concern for measles and to get instructions on how to come to the office for diagnosis without exposing other people to the virus. Measles is a highly contagious viral illness that typically begins with fever, cough, runny nose and red and watery eyes. One person with measles can easily pass it on to 9 out of 10 people around them who are unvaccinated or do not have natural immunity. Symptoms typically appear 7-14 days after contact with the virus. Tiny white spots may appear inside the mouth 2-3 days after symptoms begin. Measles rash appears 3 to 5 days after the first symptoms. It usually begins as flat red spots that appear on the face at the hairline. They then spread downward to the neck, trunk, arms, legs and feet. Measles can cause severe health complications, including pneumonia, encephalitis (inflammation of the brain) and death. Measles can be transmitted by direct contact with infectious droplets or by airborne spread when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes. The virus can remain infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to 2 hours after an infected person leaves an area. People who are infected will begin to have symptoms on average 1-2 weeks after being exposed to a person with measles. The best way to prevent getting sick is to be immunized with two doses of a measles-containing vaccine, which is primarily administered as the combination measles-mumps-rubella or MMR vaccine. Two doses of the MMR vaccine provide 97 percent protection from measles infections. Each MMR dose lowers the risk of infection and the severity of illness if infected. A small number of vaccinated people can occasionally develop measles. In these cases, the symptoms are generally milder, and they are less likely to have severe disease symptoms and spread the virus to other people. DHSS and the CDC recommend children receive one dose of MMR at 12 to 15 months of age and another at 4 to 6 years. Unvaccinated adults can also receive a “catch-up” MMR vaccination. Measles can be especially dangerous for pregnant women and their unborn babies. Children too young to be vaccinated are more likely to have severe complications if they get infected with the measles virus. Health care providers can find recommendations for infection control and diagnostic testing in the health alert issued on Sept. 4. Providers should report any suspected cases to their local health department immediately, preferably while the patient is still with the provider. More information about measles and county-level MMR vaccination rates can be found at Health.Mo.Gov/Measles . If you have any questions contact the Wright County Health Department at 417-741-7791

supplementary_news.content: US Measles Cases Top 4,200 as Pennsylvania Reports Sixth Death Related to Virus The CDC website has only recognized two of the six measles-related deaths recorded in Pennsylvania this year. Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size. Health officials in Pennsylvania have announced another death related to measles, the sixth overall in the state and the U.S. since the beginning of this year. Officials identified the person who died as a 39-year-old woman from Franklin County . The individual was reportedly not vaccinated against the virus . The county coroner described the cause of death as a “probable acute cardiac event due to possible complications of the measles.” The state is facing a large measles outbreak, accounting for about a quarter of all measles cases identified across the country since January 1, 2026. As of Tuesday morning, over 4,260 measles cases have been reported in the U.S. , 1,152 of them from Pennsylvania alone. Both South Carolina and Texas are also reporting close to 1,000 measles cases. Notably, the vast majority of people who have tested positive for measles are unvaccinated, with only 3 percent of cases affecting a person who has received the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) shot. Death from measles is rare but not unheard of, with about one to three deaths occurring for every 1,000 cases , some estimates show. The virus can also cause lifetime neurological and/or respiratory issues . Related Story “Even if I got hit by a truck tonight, HHS will never go back to what it was before,” Robert F. Kennedy Jr. bragged. The vaccine is widely considered the best way to prevent measles infection. In rare instances where a “breakthrough” case occurs (where a person who was vaccinated still gets infected), the symptoms are generally less severe . The shot requires a higher threshold of vaccinated individuals in a given community than other vaccines to be highly effective at stopping the virus’s spread. Despite a spate of deaths in Pennsylvania being recorded by state officials , the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has so far only recognized two of those deaths on its website . Measles was once considered “virtually eliminated” in the U.S., due to extremely low counts of infections identified yearly — in 2024, for instance, only 285 cases were documented . But anti-vaxxer and right-wing movements over the past couple of decades have decreased vaccine rates among the populace, resulting in much higher numbers of measles cases over the past two years. The Trump administration has also gutted programs that have been successful in getting more people vaccinated in the past. Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., himself an anti-vaxxer, has placed anti-vaxxers on health advisory panels , and recently indicated to anti-vaccine groups that his work is not yet done. “Let me be clear. You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House,” Kennedy said during a gathering of anti-vaxxers last month . Mike has also written and produced content for Vox Media and the Mon Valley Independent. He often covers breaking news, sports, and crime, among other topics. Read Full Bio Mike Darnay Updated on: October 12, 2026 / 11:41 AM EDT / CBS Pittsburgh Add CBS News on Google A 39-year-old woman in Franklin County, Pennsylvania, has died after being diagnosed with measles, officials said. The Franklin County Coroner's Office said that the woman died Saturday and that she had several underlying conditions, including a past diagnosis of measles with treatment. "This is the first death in Franklin County in many years with a patient with a recent history of a measles diagnosis and meets the definition set forth by the Pennsylvania Department of Health for a measles-associated death," the coroner's office said. The coroner's office said it is not releasing any additional details surrounding the case that could identify the individual and no indication was given as to whether the woman was vaccinated or not. This is the sixth measles-associated death in Pennsylvania so far this year. In 2026, Pennsylvania has reported a total of 1,136 cases, 157 of which have been reported within the last seven days. Measles vaccine The measles-mumps-rubella, or MMR, vaccine is safe and remains the best way to protect against measles, health officials say. The measles outbreak has prompted a growing number of people to get vaccinated. State healthcare centers have administered more than 5,500 MMR vaccinations since April in communities affected by the outbreak, and nurses have given more than 8,500 doses of the vaccine at pop-up clinics across Pennsylvania. Health experts say it may get worse. Five probable cases were reported in Rock County. It's the third cluster of cases in Wisconsin unrelated to the outbreak in the southwest region By Hope Kirwan October 15, 2026 A nurse, prepares a combination measles, mumps and rubella vaccine for a patient at a pediatrics clinic in Easley, S.C., March 17, 2026. AP Photo/Mary Conlon, File Wisconsin health officials have identified yet another cluster of measles cases this year. The state Department of Health Services on Tuesday reported five suspected cases in Rock County. Officials are still investigating how the new infections started. But Wisconsin has already seen similar clusters of cases this year. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. LinkedIn This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged. Email Chippewa County now has 11 confirmed cases after first identifying one infection related to out-of-state travel in late September. In Marathon County, six cases of measles have been confirmed since a single infection from out-of-state travel was found one month ago. Of the 267 cases reported in Wisconsin this year, the vast majority have been linked to the ongoing outbreak in the southwestern region. But Dr. Jim Conway, medical director for UW Health Immunization program, said it’s not surprising that unrelated cases are popping up given the level of measles activity around the country. Since measles was declared eliminated in the U.S. in 2000, Conway said the cases that have been identified have been isolated to local outbreaks. “Because we had relatively high immunization rates, they were manageable,” he said. “What we’ve now seen over this last 18 to 24 months is this evolution, where it’s starting to act more like what we call an endemic disease, which means it’s circulating in multiple places at multiple times, and then you’re going to get these sort of spinoffs.” Conway credits state and local health officials with keeping these cases from turning into larger outbreaks by quickly and thoroughly identifying those who have been exposed to the highly-contagious virus. Measles is the most contagious infection, according to pediatric infectious disease specialist Dr. Thomas Boyce from Marshfield Clinic Health System. He said it’s five times more contagious than COVID-19, and even a small number of cases in a community can be devastating. Children under a year old, who are not eligible for the vaccine, have the highest risk of mortality from measles, he said. “Even in an area where there’s good measles vaccine uptake, if an infant or a pregnant woman or an immunocompromised person, somebody who’s had a heart transplant or is immunosuppressed in some other way, acquires measles, it can easily be fatal,” Boyce said. “Occasionally it’s fatal even in previously healthy children.” It typically takes 11 to 12 days after someone is exposed for the first symptoms to appear — what’s referred to as the incubation period. Boyce said that means an outbreak can look like more of a prolonged smolder than an out-of-control wildfire, like the recent outbreaks in Texas and Pennsylvania. Boyce said most infectious disease doctors are worried about what will happen this winter, when the spread of all respiratory viruses picks up while people are stuck indoors. “It’s certainly ripe for bigger outbreaks than what we’re seeing right now,” he said. The virus’ long incubation period also means that public health officials have to stay alert for new infections for more than a month to ensure cases aren’t continuing to spread under the radar, according to Conway. To keep a cluster of cases from turning into a full-blown outbreak, Conway said people need to make sure they’ve received two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine, especially anyone who grew up before the recommendation of two doses was adopted in 1989. “These vaccines are extraordinarily safe and are really effective,” Conway said. “These vaccines have been around since the 1970s. I mean, we know more about these vaccines than almost any other vaccine.” Individual choice over what vaccines a person or their children receive has become increasingly important to some communities since the COVID-19 pandemic. But Boyce emphasized that the choice not to vaccinate is not inconsequential. He compares it to a parent’s choice whether to use a carseat. “You can either put your child in the car seat, or you can let them ride on your lap. But I think everyone would agree that there is only one best choice to make in that situation,” he said. “I would strongly argue that with vaccines and children, there is only one best choice, and that is to vaccinate your child with the routine vaccines that are recommended by your child’s physician.” In Wisconsin communities affected by measles, opinions on vaccines remain mixed Wisconsin Public Radio, © Copyright 2026, Board of Regents of the University of Wisconsin System and Wisconsin Educational Communications Board. Photo: Erskine Palmer/CDC/Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Pennsylvania's measles outbreak has seen cases surge past 1,130 as another death linked to the disease was announced this week. Why it matters: The death of a 39-year-old woman in Franklin County last Saturday would be the sixth measles death this year in the state. Zoom in: The woman had several underlying conditions, including a diagnosis of measles with treatment, per a news release from the Franklin County coroner's office. The coroner's office said it meets the definition of a measles-related death set by the state's health department. The coroner's office tells Axios the woman was unvaccinated. What else: Stephanie Nojiri, a spokesperson for the state's Department of Health, tells Axios that it's reviewing the death in Franklin County but has yet to confirm it's measles-related. Zoom out: Pennsylvania has seen at least 1,136 cases of measles this year as of Oct. 9, which is the worst outbreak in decades. The outbreak has largely centered on Lancaster County. The latest case figures are expected to be released later today on the state's online dashboard. What else: The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention now lists two U.S. measles deaths on its website as of Tuesday, but doesn't indicate they happened in Pennsylvania. email (opens in new window) sms (opens in new window) facebook (opens in new window) twitter (opens in new window) linkedin (opens in new window) bluesky (opens in new window) nextdoor (opens in new window) Add Axios on Google More Philadelphia stories Politics Mapped: Data center pipeline in Pennsylvania Sep 28, 2026 Go deeper (<1 min. read) Things to Do Ed Sheeran tour drama comes to Philly this weekend Sep 17, 2026 Go deeper (<1 min. read) Business By the numbers: Waymo logs big miles in Philadelphia Sep 29, 2026 Go deeper (<1 min. read) Climate Nor'easter arrives in the Philly region Sep 23, 2026 Go deeper (<1 min. read) News The bell tolls for the Academy of Natural Science's museum Sep 25, 2026 Go deeper (<1 min. read) More stories Get a free daily digest of the most important news in your backyard with Axios Philadelphia. Image courtesy of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. MILWAUKEE — The Wisconsin Department of Health Services confirms new outbreaks of measles across the state, bringing the total number of confirmed cases to 267. In Rock County, health officials have reported five probable cases that are linked to one another, but the source of the infection remains unknown. The cases are listed as probable based on the appearance of symptoms, but they have not been confirmed through lab testing. Six newly confirmed cases have been reported in Marathon County along with 11 confirmed cases in Chippewa County are related to out-of-state travel. Health department officials in both of those counties are working to “identify and notify people who may have been exposed to the measles virus”. DHS official say none of the newly confirmed or probable cases are tied to outbreak in Southwest Wisconsin that is impacting Grant, Iowa, Lafayette, and Vernon counties. Those counties are currently reporting 237 confirmed and 6 probable cases that have been spreading locally. Of the state’s 267 confirmed cases, 265 (or 99.3%) of the cases were in individuals who are not vaccinated, and 5 people have been hospitalized. DHS urges all people to check their vaccination status, as vaccination against measles through two doses of the MMR vaccine is the best way to prevent measles illness.
